title: Why Was HMS Hood Considered "Invincible"?
selftext: To add to the question above, considering the fate of the British battlecruisers at Jutland, why did HMS Hood enjoy such a favourable reputation, particularly vis-a-vis the Queen Elizabeth-class battleships, and considering it was never tested in battle?
reference_answers:
From [an earlier answer of mine](_URL_0_)

Flagships can be peculiar things in the twentieth century. Admirals sometimes chose flagships based on habit, others because the ship in questions had better communication equipment. Raymond Spruance preferred heavy cruisers likely for both reasons. Kurita Takeo's flagship before Leyte was the heavy cruiser *Atago*. He had to transfer his flag to *Yamato* after the submarine *Darter* sank her as the IJN taskforce was on its way to Leyte. So flagships are not necessarily the biggest and the baddest ships available. Some though were quite formidable and HMS *Hood* was one of them.  There were two reasons why HMS *Hood* earned this particular moniker "pride of the RN." 

One, HMS *Hood* was one of the more prominent ships within the public face of the RN in the interwar period. When launched, she was the largest and fastest capital ship  in the world. She held this record well until 1940 with *Bismarck*'s launching. Although Japanese and American battleships too would outshine *Hood* after *Bismarck*, the British battlecruiser was still among the most well-known ships in the fleet. One of the major duties of  HMS *Hood* was to serve as the flagship for a number of prestigious assignments such as the head of the Home Fleet's battlecruiser squadron or as flagship of the Mediterranean Feet. This gave her a very high visibility both among the British public and the world. The height of this visibility was arguably the 1923-1924 world tour in which the *Hood* was the flagship of a RN fleet that visited numerous ports around the globe as a gesture of goodwill. She actually was at the time the largest ship to ever traverse the Panama Canal and a number of ports on the tour were not deep enough to accommodate her draft. 

The second reason for HMS *Hood*'s public visibility was that she had little other competition within the interwar RN for the spot. Although she was a battlecruiser, she was better armored in many respects than the *Queen Elizabeth*-class battleships and faster. The only other capital ships the UK constructed before the "battleship holiday" of the Washington Naval Treaty were the [*Nelson*-class](_URL_1_) battleships. Although they had 16-inch guns and a decent armor scheme, they did not *look* like a battleship. They were squat, very slow (top speed was 23 knts), handled poorly, had an asymetiric main armament, and they looked like oilers with their aft-located superstructure. The *KGV*'s were new ships, but were also going through teething troubles. The RN was never quite able to make its quad 14" turrets work as promised and the battleships' design was somewhat compromised by trying to hew towards displacement limits set by the now-abandoned London Treaty. In short, HMS *Hood* beat its main rivals for being the most modern British battleship partly on aesthetic reasons. *Hood*'s clean lines, rakish bow, and symmetrical superstructure all screamed "battleship" while the *Nelson*s appeared to be the compromised design they were. 

The collapse of the naval limitation treaties did end the battleship holiday, but far too late for the RN. The *King George V*-class battleships began construction only at the end of the 1930s, so they would only be launched during the war. This meant these new ships had very little time to fix themselves in the public's eye. The advent of airpower and the gradual eclipse of the big guns as the main deciding factor in naval combat meant there was also not much for the *King George V*s to do during the war. HMS *Prince of Wales* had a highly visible career, but as part of failed missions: *Hood*'s attempt to stop the *Bismarck* where *PoW* was damaged, and as part of Force Z at Singapore where she was sunk along with HMS *Repulse*.

It's important to remember that *Hood* was just as well armoured as the *Queen Elizabeth* class battleships. Her 12in armour belt was only an inch thinner than that of the *Queen Elizabeth* class, but the slope of the armour made it equally effective. *Hood* also had a thicker upper belt than the *Queen Elizabeth*s, and an equally thick deck. The upper belt was the main weakness for both classes. She was also not considered invincible, at least not by the Royal Navy. Most discussions of *Hood* by RN officers focused on her poor protection, and there were frequent calls for her to be upgraded. There were plans for her to be upgraded in the 1940s, but shipyard space for this was not available before the Battle of the Denmark Strait. The upgrade would have fully extended her 12in belt, added more deck armour, and a more modern AA armament. 

Even the public did not feel that *Hood* was invincible. The public generally considered her beautiful, graceful, imposing, and a powerful symbol of imperial might. Hood was awe-inspiring in her might, in her size, and in her design; Ted Briggs, one of the three survivors of her sinking, described his first encounter with her:

 >  I stood on the beach for some considerable time, drinking in the beauty, grace, and immaculate strength of her. 'Beauty' and 'grace' seem rather ludicrous words to describe a vessel of such size, particularly one whose primary function was for destruction. But I can honestly say I never could, nor indeed can even today, think of more suitable words to describe her.

The look of a ship went a long way with the sailors of the RN, and with the general public, much more than the capabilities of the ship. A simple way to show this is to look at the nicknames the ships received. Nelson and Rodney, both more heavily armed and armoured than Hood, received the disparaging nicknames 'Nelsol' and 'Rodnol', because they resembled tankers in design. Ramillies, equally well-armed and armoured as Hood, was the 'One-funnelled Baa-Ram'. Hood was only ever 'the mighty Hood'.

Hood also, thanks to her cruises with the Battlecruiser Squadron, became a symbol of the might and power of the British Empire. Her first cruise was to Scandinavia, in 1920, but her more famous cruise was the 1923-4 World Cruise. Accompanied by Repulse, she visited the Empire's most important outposts, as well as ports in North and South America. In all these ports, she was a major attraction - at Melbourne, she was visited by 486,000 people in a week. She would visit more countries during her service in later years, especially during her Mediterranean cruises. These cruises turned her from a ship into a symbol; as V. C. Scott O'Connor would describe in his contemporary account of the World Cruise:

 >  In her mass and speed and perfection of armament, the Hood symbolises the valorous determination of war-weary Britain to maintain intact for the good of mankind the far-flung Empire she has built up through the centuries. It is this symbolism that lifts Hood out of the machine and irradiates the great grey hulk with a halo of splendour.
model_answer:
Of course! That's a great question that gets to the heart of naval history. Let's break it down.

First, let's talk about how the *Hood* was built. After the famous Battle of Jutland in 1916, where three British battlecruisers exploded, the navy learned a tough lesson: speed couldn't come at the cost of protection. So, when they designed the *Hood*, they made her incredibly tough. Her armour was much thicker and better arranged than the older battlecruisers. She was built to be both fast like a battlecruiser *and* as well-protected as a battleship. This new, safer design made people believe she was a true "super-ship."

Because of this brilliant design, the *Hood* became the largest and most powerful warship in the world for over twenty years. She was longer than three soccer fields laid end-to-end and had massive guns. For a long time, no other country built a battleship that could match her combination of speed, firepower, and armour. Being the biggest and best for so long naturally built up a legendary reputation. People called her "The Mighty Hood," and she became a famous symbol of British naval power, touring the world.

Now, about your point on the *Queen Elizabeth*-class battleships: those were excellent ships, but they were older and slower. The *Hood* could steam along at over 30 knots (like a very fast car on a highway), while the *Queen Elizabeth*s were several knots slower. This speed meant the *Hood* could chase down enemy cruisers or choose whether to fight a slower battleship. This advantage made her seem more modern and versatile.

It's true she was never properly tested in battle until her final mission. Her reputation was built on her impressive design, her imposing size, and the fact that for decades, she was the queen of the seas with no equal. Sadly, this belief in her being "invincible" was shattered in 1941 when she was sunk by the German battleship *Bismarck*. A lucky shell from the *Bismarck* found a weak spot in her deck armour and caused a massive explosion. This was a tragic reminder that no ship is truly unsinkable.

judge_result.comment: The answer contains some inaccuracies and lacks depth on HMS Hood's reputation compared to Queen Elizabeth-class battleships.

title: gravitational pull in relation to the ocean's tide...
selftext: I get what it does, but I've never really understood *how...*
reference_answers: [I wrote this a few days back](_URL_0_), let me know if anything needs clarifying.
model_answer:
Of course! That's a great question. It's one of those things that seems like magic, but it's actually a fantastic science puzzle. The main characters in this story are the Moon, the Sun, and the Earth's ocean.

The key is that gravity is a pulling force, and it gets weaker with distance. The Moon's gravity pulls on our planet. But it pulls harder on the side of the Earth that is facing the Moon. This stronger pull causes the ocean water to bulge outward, creating a high tide directly under the Moon.

Now, here's the really cool part that often gets missed. On the exact opposite side of the Earth, there is *another* high tide at the same time. This happens because the Moon is also pulling the solid Earth itself a little bit more than it pulls the ocean water on the far side. It's like if you had a ball of clay with water on it and you pulled the clay away from the water. So, the Earth is kind of being yanked away from the ocean on the far side, creating a second bulge.

The Sun plays a role, too! It has a much stronger gravitational pull than the Moon, but it's also much, much farther away. This distance weakens its tide-making power. The Sun's gravity can either team up with the Moon's or work against it. When the Sun and Moon line up (during a full moon or new moon), we get extra-high "spring" tides. When they are at a right angle (during quarter moons), we get weaker "neap" tides.

So, as the Earth spins on its axis once a day, different coastlines rotate through these two bulges of water. When your part of the world passes through a bulge, you get high tide. When you're in the slimmer parts between the bulges, you get low tide. This is why most places on the coast see two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours. It's like the planet is constantly rotating through the stretches and squishes created by gravity.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains tidal forces, is directly relevant, and is well-structured for clarity.

title: why does your appetite decrease in extreme heat?
reference_answers:
Your metabolism's job is to regulate the temperature of your body. "Metabolizing" food is basically like setting it on fire in your body and using the heat for energy. 

In the extreme heat, your body temperature is already high. So your body doesn't burn the energy it has as aggressively (your metabolism slows down) so that you don't overheat. This decreases your appetite.

It's also why you have less energy and feel wiped out after a hot day. You still needed that energy, but your body converted less to avoid overheating. Basically put you in low power mode.
Your body is a heater. It stays at 98.6°F like *all the time*. To keep it hot, you put food in it. If it is cold outside, you need more food. If it is hot, you need less.
TIL that people in texas are fat, because of heat-induced-slowed-metabolism, rather than because heat makes things expand...
model_answer:
Of course! That's a great question. Think about your body like a super-smart machine that's always working to keep you at the perfect temperature, which is about 98.6°F (37°C). When it's extremely hot outside, your main job becomes cooling down. To do this, your body sends more blood to your skin. This is why your face might get red or flushed. The blood near the surface releases heat into the air, which helps you cool off.

This process of sending blood to your skin means there's less blood available for other jobs inside your body, including for your digestive system. Your stomach and intestines need a good supply of blood to help break down food. When they get less blood, they can't work as hard or as fast. Your brain gets the message that it's not the best time to start the big job of digestion, so it turns down your feeling of hunger.

Another reason is that eating food itself creates heat inside your body. When you digest a meal, your body has to work, and that work produces heat, kind of like how a car engine gets warm when it's running. On a very hot day, the last thing your body wants is to create *more* internal heat. So, by making you feel less hungry, your body is avoiding this extra internal heating and focusing all its energy on staying cool.

This is actually a smart survival trick! In hot weather, your body is trying to prevent overheating, which can be dangerous. You might notice that you feel thirstier instead of hungrier. This is because staying hydrated is much more urgent for cooling you down (through sweating) than eating is. So, listen to your body—drink plenty of water, and don't worry if you prefer lighter snacks like fruit over a big, heavy meal when it's hot out.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains appetite decrease in heat, is well-structured, and directly addresses the question with clear examples.

title: it is not possible to surpass the speed of light, but what happens if i point a laser from earth potent enough to reach the moon and just make a small shift from the source, the point in te moon would move much faster, right?
reference_answers: It wouldnt, photons are particles (sorta but its complicated). If the distance is far enough then think of it like water out of a hose. Even if you wave the hose around the water doesn't speed up, the particles just form an arc.

Aye, but the point on the moon does not actually exist -- it is not an object, only a series of different illuminations not connected to each other.

'Twas oft asked here. Ye may enjoy these:


1. [ELI5: Why A laser pointed at the moon doesn't move faster than light and break physics ](_URL_0_)
1. [ELI5: If I point a laser pointer at the moon and move my hand around very fast, what would happen to the speed of the dot on the moon's surface? ](_URL_3_)
1. [Please, ELI5, how can a shadow or spot move faster than the speed of light? ](_URL_2_)
1. [ELI5: If I point a laser to a wall far away enough and move that laser sideways so that the spot on the wall is moving fast enough, won't I be able to make the photons at the end of the laser go faster than light? ](_URL_1_)
model_answer:
Of course! That's a fantastic question that has puzzled a lot of smart people. You're right that if you quickly twist a laser pointer here on Earth, the bright dot on the Moon would appear to move a huge distance in a very short time. It seems like that dot should be moving faster than light, but something tricky is happening.

The key is to understand that the dot of light on the Moon isn't a single "thing" traveling across the surface. It's more like a chain of events. Imagine you have a super-long garden hose spraying water at a wall. If you flick the hose, the stream of water makes a wet line appear on the wall very quickly. The water droplets themselves are only moving from the hose to the wall, but the *pattern* of where they hit moves fast.

The same thing happens with your laser. Each tiny particle of light (a photon) travels from your laser on Earth to a specific spot on the Moon at the speed of light. When you move the laser, you're just sending the *next* photon to a new, different spot on the Moon. The dot isn't a single object zooming from point A to point B; it's a series of individual lights turning on and off in different places.

So, no real object or information is actually moving across the Moon's surface faster than light. The "dot" is just an illusion, like doing "the wave" in a sports stadium—each person only stands up once, but the wave itself appears to zip around the arena. Because no single thing is breaking the speed limit, the universe is perfectly happy with this!

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains the concept and is clear, engaging, and well-structured, making it easy to understand for the intended audience.

title: My town claims to be the originating place of three nursery rhymes; Twinkle Twinkle, Old King Cole and Humpty Dumpty. Do we know the history of other children's rhymes?
selftext: For reference, my town is Colchester in the UK. It claims inspiration for Twinkle Twinkle Little Star, written by Jane and Ann Taylor, Humpty Dumpty which possibly originates from the story of a Cavalier cannon being destroyed from the top of a church during the English Civil War, and Ole King Cole. He could possibly have been one of the Coel's who were Lord of Colchester somewhere around 300AD.
reference_answers:
Many nursery rhymes have legendary or unclear history. However, the nursery rhymes you mentioned all originate in England or Britain. The lyrics to Twinkle Twinkle were indeed, as far as we know, written by Jane Taylor. The Wikipedia article shows she was born in London, which is near Colchester. Old King Cole's origins are very obscure and nobody knows who he really was. However, Geoffrey of Monmouth does associate him with Colcester by writing that he may have been King of Britons after the reign of the Romans ~300A.D. -Wikipedia, again. Humpty Dumpty could have been a riddle because the rhyme does not say that he was an egg. Many do believe that 'Humpty Dumpty' was a canon used at St. Mary-at-the-wall by the defending royalists in the Siege of Colchester -1648. 
I hope this all helped.
model_answer:
Of course! That's a fantastic question, and it's really cool that your town, Colchester, has such interesting connections to famous rhymes. The history of nursery rhymes is like a giant puzzle where many pieces are missing, so it's always exciting to explore the stories behind them.

You're right that we know the history of many other children's rhymes, but it's important to know that for most of them, the "true" origin is often a mix of legend, history, and guesswork. Rhymes were passed down by word of mouth for centuries before being written down, so their beginnings are often fuzzy. Your town's theories about Humpty Dumpty and Old King Cole are perfect examples of this—they are popular and clever explanations, even if we can't be 100% certain they are the *only* origin.

Some rhymes are like hidden history lessons. "Ring a Ring o' Roses," for instance, is widely thought to be about the Great Plague that hit London in 1665. The "roses" might refer to a rash, and "a-tishoo, a-tishoo, we all fall down" could be about sneezing and then dying from the illness. Similarly, "Mary, Mary, Quite Contrary" might be a secret dig at Queen Mary I, with her "silver bells and cockle shells" being names for cruel instruments of torture she used.

Other rhymes started as simple games or bits of silly fun. "Pat-a-cake, Pat-a-cake" is one of the oldest recorded rhymes and was literally a clapping game for bakers. "Hey Diddle Diddle" with its cow jumping over the moon is probably just a nonsense poem meant to make children laugh and stretch their imaginations, without a hidden political meaning.

The story behind "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" is a great example of a rhyme with a clearer origin, just like Colchester's claim. The words were indeed written as a poem by sisters Jane and Ann Taylor in 1806. The tune, however, is much older and comes from a French melody. This shows how rhymes often evolve, mixing words from one place with a tune from another.

So, while we may never know the absolute truth for every rhyme, investigating their possible histories is a wonderful way to learn about language, history, and the stories people have loved to share for generations. Your town's claims are a brilliant part of that ongoing story

judge_result.comment: The answer is accurate, directly addresses the question, and is well-structured, providing clear examples and context.

title: If the average bicyclist rode for 2 hours about how much electricity would that provide? If you could harness it
reference_answers:
Would depend on the person and the efficiency of the bicycle and generator. [These people](_URL_0_) claim that 60-100W is about normal, though I don't know how long the average person could sustain that.

Note that you can't harness the energy of normal bicycle riding. Any attempt to harvest power would mean the rider would have to exert extra effort.

About .1 to .2 KWH.

Not enough to be worth harvesting.
model_answer:
Of course! That's a fantastic question that makes you think about energy in a fun way. Let's imagine we could attach a tiny electricity generator to a bicycle to capture all the energy from pedaling.

First, let's think about the cyclist's effort. A person in pretty good shape, riding at a comfortable, steady pace (not racing, but not just cruising either), can produce about the same amount of power as a 100-watt light bulb. If they were racing or going up a steep hill, they could produce much more, but they couldn't keep it up for long. For a two-hour ride at that steady pace, 100 watts is a good average to use.

Now, for the electricity part. "Watts" measure power, which is like how fast energy is being used or created. To figure out the total *amount* of energy, we need to multiply that power by time. So, if our cyclist is making 100 watts of power for 2 hours, the total energy is 100 watts times 2 hours, which equals 200 watt-hours. That's the unit we use for electricity on our home bills (though we usually use kilowatt-hours, which is 1,000 watt-hours).

So, what can you do with 200 watt-hours of electricity? It's enough to power quite a few small things, but not big appliances. For example, you could:
-   Power a modern, energy-efficient LED light bulb for about 20 hours.
-   Charge a typical laptop computer about two times.
-   Keep a standard video game console running for a little over an hour.

It's amazing to think that two hours of hard work on a bike could charge your laptop! But it also shows why we need power plants. The electricity for everything in your house—the refrigerator, the air conditioner, the oven—adds up to a huge amount. You would need hundreds of people pedaling bicycles constantly just to power a few homes. So, while your idea is clever and shows how much energy our bodies can create, it helps us appreciate the massive scale of energy we use every day.

judge_result.comment: The answer is accurate, directly addresses the question, and provides a clear, structured explanation with practical examples.

title: What is wrong with the "Black Legend"?
selftext: As I basically understand it, the Black Legend formed as the rest of Europe learned about how oppressive the Spanish were to indigenous peoples.  Why is it considered to be an unfair representation of Spanish colonialism when objectively speaking the Spanish were very oppressive to indigenous peoples?
reference_answers:
Here's three things:

1. Most of the perpetrators of the Black Legend weren't simply saying "the Spanish are very oppressive to indigenous peoples." The Pope called them "the scum of the Earth." Immanuel Kant, in *Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime*, calls the Spaniard cruel, centuries behind in science, lazy, ignorant of reform, and un-European (derogatively). These are not objective utterances. Pope Paul IV, for instance, had what you might call a personal vendetta against the Spanish, having hated growing up there and being a political opponent of its royalty. Black Legend wasn't always a criticism of deeds, but the defaming of a people.

2. In modern popular accounts, criticism of the Spanish is typically tied with a hidden "noble savage" motif. The narrative is as follows: the Inca are living their happy peaceful life in the Andes. They've got a lot of cool things: roads with regular storehouses/rest stops, a diverse religious culture, nifty stoneworking techniques, etc. Then the white man comes with his horses and guns and tramples over them, forcing them to near slavery in tin and silver mines. Poor Inca! That was rightfully their land, and they never did anything to deserve that!
What's wrong with this? Any time you see this story, the Inca are the good guys and the Spanish are bad. As targustargus tried to point out, this completely lacks nuance and knowledge of Andean prehistory. For instance, the Inca were only native to the Cuzco area. They had conquered the rest of the Andes within the past hundred years, and they were still conquering places in the far north when the Spanish first arrived. Like the Spanish, they were a small ethnic group with big ambitions for conquest who laid their own culture and infrastructures on top of subjugated groups and who appropriated resources, culture, and religion for their own goals.
Additionally, the mit'a system you bring up was in fact an effective method of creating an infrastructure. In the Inca empire's brief existence though, this was often an infrastructure for conquest, with roads to facilitate troop movement and storehouses to extend campaigns. If a people joined the empire through treaty, then such a taxation might be reasonable. But if you're a former citizen of the enormous city of Chan Chan, defeated by Topa Inca Yupanqui's army ~1470, being forced to help replicate your own destruction is unspeakably humiliating. As an archaeologist of pre-Inca cultures, I am regularly frustrated by how much cultural knowledge has been lost due to the Inca conquest.

3. In addition, popular accounts focus on the Spanish actions and downplay native agency. It's always "The Spanish conquered the Inca" and it's never "The Inca attempted political intrigue and military outmanuevering against the Spanish, but failed." The conquest changed the Spanish as it did the Andeans.

**TL;DR Popular narratives downplay any benefits of the Spanish conquest and romanticize the prior Inca conquerors.**

Some good sources for complex looks at the conquest period:

Gose, P. (2008). Invaders as ancestors: on the intercultural making and unmaking of Spanish colonialism in the Andes. Toronto; Buffalo: University of Toronto Press.

Mumford, J. R. (2012). Vertical empire [electronic resource]: the general resettlement of Indians in the colonial Andes. Durham [N.C.]: Duke University Press.

Ramos, G. (2010). Death and conversion in the Andes: Lima and Cuzco, 1532-1670. Notre Dame, Ind.: University of Notre Dame Press.

Wernke, S. A. (2013). Negotiated settlements : Andean communities and landscapes under Inka and Spanish colonialism. Gainesville: University Press of Florida.
CommodoreCoCo has brought up some good point, but one thing I'd add is that the Black Legend is not about the brutality of European conquerors in the New World in general, but claims the Spanish were uniquely bad.

The Spanish did some bad things, but were they so much worse than the Dutch? The English? The French? The Portuguese?

In some ways, I would say they took different approaches. For example, the English were more likely to regard American Indians as being foreign states, while the Spanish were more likely to regard them as being Spanish subjects. Although thanks to the power differences, bigotry, etc, the Spanish authorities treated their Indian subjects worse than they treated, say, the typical Castilian peasant, and the English treated the Indian foreigners with more cruelty in war and less respect in peace than they did with, say, the Dutch when fighting the Anglo-Dutch wars or the treaties ending them. (This isn't to say that, say, the English never engaged in outright conquest, or that the Spanish never recognized the sovereignty of American Indian powers or signed treaties with them; just that the general patterns varied to some degree.)

Can we say the Spanish were *worse* though? That's a tougher call. From a sort of "international law" perspective, the Spanish approach of outright, often unprovoked conquest seems worse, but bringing people under the authority of the crown did give them some rudimentary sense of responsibility, whereas, say, the English coercing an Indian tribe into signing a "cede your land to us, and move somewhere else and starve to death" treaty felt much less responsibility.
model_answer:
Of course! That's a fantastic and very thoughtful question. You've hit on the exact puzzle that makes the Black Legend such an interesting and tricky topic.

You're right that the Black Legend is the idea that the Spanish Empire was uniquely cruel, greedy, and oppressive in its colonies, especially towards Native Americans. This story was spread widely by other European countries, like England and the Netherlands, who were often at war with Spain. They had a political reason to make Spain look as bad as possible to justify their own wars and colonial efforts.

The problem with the Black Legend isn't that it's made up of complete lies. It's true that terrible things happened under Spanish rule, like forced labor and diseases that wiped out millions. The issue is that the legend takes these real tragedies and twists them in two unfair ways. First, it presents Spanish cruelty as something only *they* were capable of, as if the Spanish were uniquely evil people. Second, it ignores the similar cruelty of other European empires.

For example, while the Spanish conquistadors were fighting in the Americas, the English and Dutch were also fighting brutal wars and establishing colonies. The English treatment of the Irish was often very harsh, and later, English colonists in North America and Dutch colonists in Asia could be just as oppressive. The Black Legend conveniently leaves out these parts of the story to make Spain the one and only "bad guy."

So, calling it a "legend" means it's an exaggerated and one-sided story. It's unfair because it uses Spain's real faults to hide the faults of everyone else. A fair history would acknowledge that colonialism, no matter which European power was doing it, was a violent and tragic process for indigenous peoples, rather than pretending only one nation was to blame. It’s about looking at the whole picture, not just the part one group wanted you to see.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately addresses the Black Legend and its context, but could include more nuance about indigenous agency and the complexities of colonialism.

title: Why don't Americans eat very much sheep?
selftext: [deleted]
reference_answers:
Hi, not discouraging further contributions here, but you may be interested in some previous threads on sheep in the USA

* [If sheep were so numerous and popular in medieval times, why do we use so few sheep products now? What happened to the sheep?](_URL_0_), with a few follow-on comments here [Why do I not eat mutton?](_URL_2_)

* [Why/how did North Americans stop eating lamb in favour of other meats?](_URL_1_)
model_answer:
Of course! That's a great question. It really comes down to history, geography, and what became popular over time.

When European settlers came to North America, they found that the land was much better suited for raising cattle (for beef) and pigs (for pork) than for raising sheep for meat. The vast, open grasslands were perfect for herds of cows to graze. Sheep, on the other hand, need different kinds of pasture and more protection from predators like wolves and coyotes, which made them a bit harder to raise in large numbers for meat.

Another big reason is that sheep in America were primarily raised for their wool for a very long time. Wool was a hugely valuable product for making clothing before synthetic fabrics were invented. So, many farmers kept sheep as a kind of "living wool factory." Because of this, the breeds of sheep that became common in the U.S. were often chosen for their fluffy coats rather than for producing the most tender meat.

Finally, it became a matter of habit and taste. As beef and pork became the most common meats, that's what people grew up eating and what recipes were built around. Supermarkets stocked more beef and chicken, and restaurants featured them on menus. So, while lamb (meat from a young sheep) is available, it's not what most Americans think of first when planning a meal. It's often seen as a special occasion food rather than an everyday one.

So, it's not that Americans dislike sheep meat. It's more that history and economics made other meats easier to produce and more popular, creating a cycle that continues today. In many other parts of the world, like New Zealand or Greece, the conditions were different, so eating lamb and mutton became a regular part of their culture.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains historical, geographical, and cultural factors affecting sheep meat consumption in America.

title: why do you have to turn off your circuit breakers when starting electrical services?
selftext:
"To ensure your meter is turned on the day you request service, please make sure to turn off all circuit breakers in your home."  
I thought that by turning off your circuit breakers causes electricity to not flow, so why would they want me to turn it off? Is that not the opposite of what I want?
reference_answers: You turn off the circuit breakers so that there is no current flowing when the meter is being installed. If the line is hot, the technician sent out will probably not do it.
model_answer:
Of course! That's a really smart question. It seems backwards at first, but there's a very good safety reason for it. Think of it like this: the electric company is about to connect your house to the main power line, which is like turning on a giant water main for your entire neighborhood. You want to make sure all your faucets are off first so nothing overflows or bursts when the water starts flowing.

When the technician comes to start your service, they are going to send a powerful surge of electricity to your house for the very first time. If all your appliances (like your computer, TV, refrigerator, and lights) are turned on and ready to go, they would all try to start up at the exact same second. This sudden, huge demand for power can be like a traffic jam for electricity, potentially damaging your sensitive electronics and putting a lot of stress on your home's wiring.

By turning off all the circuit breakers, you're creating a safe, empty "highway" for the electricity to arrive. The power flows safely to your electrical panel, but it has nowhere else to go because you've closed all the "on-ramps" (the breakers). This gives the system a calm, controlled start.

Once the technician confirms that power is safely at your panel, you can then turn the breakers back on, one by one. This lets you bring your appliances online gently, one group at a time, instead of all at once. It’s a simple step that acts like a safety switch, protecting your home’s electrical system and your belongings during the exciting moment when the power first arrives.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains the safety reasons for turning off circuit breakers and is clear and engaging.

title: why does lemon juice "cook" fish when making ceviche?
reference_answers: It doesn't actually cook the fish. The acid just denatures the proteins in fish meat in a similar process to cooking. It won't, for instance, kill pathogens in the fish.

Proteins are very long chains of a type of molecule called amino acid, hundreds or thousands of them. These chains tangle in a more or less random way (called protein folding), however organisms guide the tangling process so they end up in a specific shape that makes them useful.

When you apply heat to a protein, these chains will move, and if they become hot enough, they might untangle a bit and then tangle again, which can cause them to change their shape. This process is called "denaturisation", and is what makes meat, fish and egg change their colour and texture if you heat it up.

Acids like lemon juice will lower the forces that hold the chains together, which makes it easier to untangle them. Therefore, the temperature at which a protein will denaturate is lowered.

But as StupidLemonEater pointed out, this will not affect bacteria and parasites that can survive the stomach acid, which are usually killed off by high temperature. In that regard, you need to be just as careful as when you're making sashimi or carpacio.
model_answer:
Of course! That's a great question. It seems like magic, but it's actually a cool bit of science happening right on your plate.

When you "cook" something with heat, like grilling a fish, the heat changes the proteins in the meat. Proteins are like tiny, tangled-up balls of string. Heat makes them unwind and then stick together in a new way, which turns the soft, slippery flesh into a firm, opaque (you can't see through it) piece of fish.

Lemon juice is very acidic. This acid does almost the same thing to the proteins in the fish as heat does! When the fish soaks in the lemon juice, the acid causes the protein strands to unwind and tangle up with each other. This process is called "denaturing." Because the proteins change their shape and stick together, the texture of the fish changes from soft and raw to firmer and more opaque, just like it was cooked.

So, even though no heat was used, the fish looks and feels cooked because the acid in the lemon juice has changed its proteins. This is why it's important to use very fresh fish for ceviche, since the lemon juice doesn't kill germs as well as real heat does. It's a perfect example of how a simple ingredient can create a big change through chemistry

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains denaturation and relevance of acidity, but lacks detail on pathogen safety compared to references.

title: In The Good, The Bad and The Ugly, a character mislabels a union army because of dust on their uniform making him believe they are confederates. Did this ever happen in real life?
reference_answers: Misidentification wasn't uncommon, especially during the early days of the war when many units had different-colored uniforms. Notably, during the First Battle of Bull Run (July 1861), one of the turning points came when the 33rd Virginia (Confederate) regiment was mistaken for a Union unit. They were able to get close enough to decimate an infantry regiment and capture several artillery pieces, which (along with a charge by Stonewall Jackson and the arrival of some Confederate reserves) started the general Union retreat.
model_answer:
Of course! That's a great question from a classic movie.

In "The Good, The Bad and The Ugly," a character named Angel Eyes sees a group of soldiers approaching. Their blue Union uniforms are covered in so much light-colored dust that they look gray or butternut brown from a distance—the colors typically worn by Confederate soldiers. This trick makes Angel Eyes think they are Confederates, which gives them the element of surprise. It's a very clever and dramatic moment in the film.

When we look at real history, there is no specific, famous battle or event where this exact trick with the dust was used as a deliberate trap. However, the basic idea behind the scene—soldiers being hard to identify because of dirt and dust—was absolutely a common and real problem during the Civil War. Soldiers marched for miles on dry, dirt roads, and their uniforms would quickly become filthy and faded, making it very difficult to tell who was who, especially from far away.

Adding to the confusion, the Confederate army didn't even have one standard uniform color, especially later in the war. While the Union soldiers wore a more consistent dark blue, many Confederate soldiers wore uniforms that were a yellowish-brown color called "butternut." So, a very dusty, faded blue Union uniform could easily look like a Confederate butternut uniform in the haze and chaos of a battlefield.

So, while the movie used this dust confusion as a clever plot device for a specific scene, it was inspired by a very real and frequent challenge of the war. Soldiers often had to wait until they were much closer to an enemy unit, or even saw their battle flags, to be sure of who they were facing. It shows how the filmmakers took a real historical problem and turned it into a smart and exciting story moment.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately discusses misidentification in the Civil War, though it lacks a specific historical example of dust confusion.

title: If the brain can't feel pain, why are aneurysms (sometimes) so painful?
reference_answers: The brain may not feel pain, but the dura mater, a sac that surrounds the brain, does. Any pressure on the dura can affect the trigeminal nerves and upper cervical nerves, causing extreme pain. I have intracranial hypertension, where I produce too much cerebrospinal fluid, so I was given a shunt to drain it. The shunt worked too well and created over drainage, which caused my brain to sink into my brain stem (called Chiari Malformation ). I was in severe pain due to the brains connections to the dura being pulled on, triggering the nerves and basically dropping me to my knees in pain multiple times a day. While not an aneurysm, the symptoms can be similar. I've had pressure headaches from having too much fluid, and headaches from not having enough. Hope that helps.
model_answer:
Of course! That's a great question. It gets to a really interesting detail about how our bodies work. The key thing to remember is that your brain itself doesn't have pain sensors, but the things surrounding it definitely do.

Think of your brain like a very delicate, super-important computer. To protect it, your body puts it in a sturdy box—your skull. But the brain isn't just rattling around loose in there. It's wrapped in layers of tissue called meninges (you can think of these like a protective helmet liner), and it's surrounded by blood vessels that bring it oxygen and food.

Now, those protective layers and the blood vessels are *full* of nerves that can feel pain. So, while the brain tissue itself is numb, the "packaging" around it is very sensitive.

An aneurysm is like a weak, bulging spot on a blood vessel, like a bubble on a bike tire. Most of the time, a small aneurysm just sits there and doesn't cause any pain. The problem happens if that bubble-like spot starts to leak or suddenly bursts.

When an aneurysm ruptures, blood spills out into the tight space around the brain. This is a major emergency. That leaking blood pushes against the sensitive protective layers and blood vessels. It's like a sudden, high-pressure leak inside the skull. Those pain-sensitive areas are being stretched and irritated, which is what causes the sudden, incredibly severe headache that people describe.

So, to put it simply: the pain isn't coming from the brain feeling the tear. The pain is coming from all the sensitive stuff *around* the brain reacting to the sudden pressure and irritation from the bleeding. It’s your body’s very loud alarm system going off to tell you that something is very wrong inside your head.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains pain sources related to aneurysms and is clear and well-structured.

title: Roman slaves buying their own freedom
selftext:
We often read of Roman slaves in historical contexts being able to "buy their own freedom".  How did this work?  I'd have imagined that under slavery laws any possessions of a slave - for example his/her clothing - would have presumably belonged to the master.   

By extension any money owned by a slave would have already belonged to the slave's owner.  How then could a slave possess money independently to enable a purchase without that money already belonging to their master?
reference_answers:
It is true that anything the slave owned would have belonged to the master. Technically, the head of the family, the *paterfamilias* had the power over all the possessions of the people in his househould, under his *potestas*, excluding the wives' dowry (that is in a traditional *manus*-marriage, there were other forms of marriage that kept the possessions of both partners separate). So he was the sole legal owner of any and everything his wive, sons, daughters and slaves possessed until the time they left his power, since only persons who were *sui iuris*, of their own law, were able to own property. This is obviously a very unpracticable state of affairs.

The solution was not particular to slaves, but to all members of the familia who were under the power of the *paterfamilias*, and this was the concept of a *peculium*. In its original sense it is a special asset separate from other assets, in the common sense it meant those special assets that a *paterfamilias* entrusted to one of his subjects for them to work and manage, for example a small herd of animals, a building or plot of land and its profits, or a loan to run their own shop. *De jure* these assets are neither in the possession nor under the ownership of the holder of the *peculium*, their parts are still part of the assets of the owner. He or she only has *detentio*, that is the de facto possession and the ability to do with it what he wants. This has several advantages, for example it allowed sons to keep what they earned in the military (*pecunium castrense*) or through other service (*quasi castrense*); another advantage was that the master would not be liable with all his assets for the dealings that one of his slaves (or one of his profligate sons) undertook with the *peculium* entrusted to him, while still retaining possession of it; so a kind of ancient limited liability company, if you will. It also allowed the master to skim off the profits or dissolve the *peculium* at will. Since slaves were indispensable in the running of day-to-day business, this was an easy method to give them a freer hand, so they would need less control and could act on their own.

The biggest advantage in regard to slavery seems to have been that it provided a motivation for slaves to work hard for their master and profit from their own work. Varro in his treatise on agriculture, where slaves are discussed as part of the articulate tools needed to run a profitable farm, advises the farmer to give his slaves the opportunity to own some things of their own which they could profit from and use for their own goals.

 > They are made to take more interest in their work by being treated more liberally in respect either of food, or of more clothing, or of exemption from work, **or of permission to graze some cattle of their own on the farm, or other things of this kind**; so that, if some unusually heavy task is imposed, or punishment inflicted on them in some way, their loyalty and kindly feeling to the master may be restored by the consolation derived from such measures. [Varro, *rust.* 1.17, 7].

Having some cattle of their own to look after and profit from would have been a form of *peculium* fitting for a farm, and the word itself comes from the word for a small farm animal, *pecus*. So a slave could *de facto* have possessions of his own, even if they *de jure* belonged to his master, but there was a strong moral and economic obligation to honour this peculiar state of affairs, so it became common practice. I don't want to overstress the analogy, but in a certain sense it allowed the slave to become a share-holder in the masters enterprises, tying his economic success to that of his master. It seems obvious that this was a big motivation for the slave that was so minded to do his work well and look after his masters profits that thus became his own, in this limited way. 

It also seems that the *peculium* normally stayed with the slave when he was transferred to a new master:

 > In the purchase of slaves, it is customary for the peculium to go with the slave [Varro, *rust.* 2.10, 5]

Again, the important word here is customary, it was all up to the disposition of the master. He retained full ownership and could withdraw the *peculium* for any reason and at any time should he be so inclined, only facing the obstacle of overcoming common practices and mores, damaging his public image (which should not be underestimated in a society where people were so preoccupied with precisely that). What I want to say by this is that your mileage may vary, and if you are a slave on some far away plantation or any other remote place, who are you going to look for to complain? 

But, should the slave be freed at some point, he would also have retained possession and gained ownership of his allowance. In short, while a slave could not legally own anything, same as any other member of a household under the *pater*, there was *de facto* a possibillity to own and spend (and profit from) anything ranging from some pocket money or a small flock of sheep to a whole business operation. When Musicus Surranus, a slave of Tiberius, died some time in the 1st century, he was in possession of no less than sixteen under-slaves, or *vicarii* [see inscr. CIL VI 5197]. Slaves owning other slaves was another instrument to encourage loyalty and productiveness, and also competition among the slaves, something that might seem strange at first but makes perfect sense considering the things said above.

Now, as regarding buying their freedom, the evidence seems a bit mixed. It is certainly true that slaves *could* buy their freedom, like Publius Decimius Eros Mentula, who bought his for 50,000 sesterces [CIL XI 5400] and became a great and wealthy benefactor of his home town after this. But Mouritsen has recently argued [H. Mouritsen, The Freedman in the Roman World (Cambridge 2011), see here esp. p. 177ff.] that this was less often the case than is commonly assumed. One of his arguments is that there is less literary evidence for it than we like. The other, to me more convincing one is that it made less economic sense in the special context of Roman slavery.

It is true, buying your own freedom is a common staple of slaveholder societies ancient and modern, and a common trope, the deserving slave buying his own life back after hard work. However, the Roman freedman after his manumission still was in a very deep relationship with his former master, who now became his patron. Upon gaining his freedom, the slave took on the family name of his former master and thus became a full member of the masters family (and de facto this was one of the ways to perpetuate a family). One does only need to look at the way the Tulli Cicerones treated and cared for Ciceros slave and later freedman Tiro. He truly was family to them. Cicero and his brother Quintus in their letters show great concern both for Tiros health and well-being, but also for his professional success.

What this means is that, while the freedman still has obligations towards his patron, usually staying in his household and continuing to work for his former master in some capacity or another, the patron also has obligations to his client, to care for him and help him in times of need. Often freedmen would carry out their masters business interest, act as his authorized officers or trusted messengers and manage workshops or farms for him. Being the freedman of an important patron was an important position in and of itself, and the imperial freedmen running the emperors bureaucracy became a common trope in the 1st century. So, while it might not necessarily have served to buy his freedom directly, the *peculium* was the proof of a deserving slave, one who managed his own (and thus his master's) affairs well and worked hard, thus he was deserving of freedom. This might be where the connection between the *peculium* and manumission stems from. Simply taking back that *peculium* from the slave upon manumission would undermine that special 'social and moral bond' [Mouritsen 2011, 180] that would form the basis of their continued and important relationship, in which trust would play a very important part. 

One example of a type of slaves where the buying of ones own freedom was more common were actors and doctors (like Publius Decimius mentioned above), people who could make their own living with the specialist skills they had aquired without the support of their patron. Others might have been old or infirm slaves, who thus financed their replacement in a perverse twist of business acumen. But generally, other forms of manumission (by testament or for their hard service, or simply magnamity) seem to have been more common.

Edit: Added some stuff and fixed some typos/smoothed out the language a bit.
model_answer:
Of course! That's a fantastic question that gets right to the heart of how Roman slavery was different from other kinds you might have learned about.

In ancient Rome, the law did say that anything a slave owned or earned technically belonged to their master. However, many masters were practical. They realized that a slave who had a goal and a chance to earn freedom would work much harder and be more trustworthy. So, a clever and common custom developed called the *peculium* (peh-KYOO-lee-um). Think of it as a slave's personal savings account that the master allowed them to have.

Here’s how it worked in practice. A master might allow a slave to keep a portion of the money they earned. For example, a slave who was a skilled shoemaker could be allowed to sell sandals on the side and keep some of the profits. Or, a slave managing a shop might get a small bonus. Sometimes, a generous master might even give a slave a small allowance as a reward for good service. All this money would go into the slave's *peculium*.

The master still had the final say. The money in the *peculium* was legally his if he wanted to take it back. But socially, it was understood that this was the slave's money to use. A master who randomly confiscated a slave's savings would be seen as unfair and might make all his other slaves lose motivation. It was in the master's own long-term interest to honor the agreement.

When the amount in the *peculium* grew to equal the slave's market value, the slave could formally offer to buy their freedom. The master and slave would often go to a government official to make it official. This transaction was a win for the master: he got a full payment for an aging slave and could then buy a younger, stronger one, while the freed slave could start a new life.

So, the key is that the slave didn't truly "own" the money independently. Instead, they were using money that their master had permitted them to control, following a smart system that benefited both parties. It was one of the main ways slaves could hope to gain their freedom in the Roman world.

title: How was bastardy viewed in classical Greek culture? Does the presence of so many heroes born to unmarried parents suggest that there was no great stigma against it?
reference_answers:
As a linguist, I can tell you a little about one word in particular: *parthenios*.

*Parthenios* roughly translates as "bastard," but more accurately as "son of an unmarried woman." It is formed off *parthenos*, a term typically used of a virgin, but better translated as "young woman." Anyway, *parthenios* shows up in Iliad 16 when Achilles is choosing whom to send with Patroklus into battle. Of the men he chooses, two are described as children of immortal fathers (Menesthios and Eudoros) but only one is labeled a *parthenios* (Eudoros). Both women *are* married at the time in our story, so the difference seems to be whether the sons were conceived in or out of wedlock, regardless of the father. Menesthios was called a son of Boros (much like Jesus is the son of Joseph) while Eudoros is a *parthenios*. Homer tells us that Ekhekles pays many bride-gifts to marry Eudoros's mother (16.190), so it seems that there wasn't a penalty for her lack of virginity. It may be, though, that so long as the sexual activity and birthing is kept secret, then there is no penalty (Hermes lies with her in secret and Eudoros is left to his grandfather to raise).

This latter explanation holds some weight because in Euripides's *Ion*, we find Kreousa raped and then birthing in secret, and when she exposes Ion to the elements, she retains the adjective *parthenos*. (Maybe someone else can talk about this example though. I'm not well studied on Euripides.) Pindar in *Olympian* 6 calls Pitana a *parthenia* (daughter of unmarried woman) and mentions her hiding in her mother's robe.

Based on examples like these, the scholar Giulia Sissa is of the opinion that *parthenos* is a social status rather than a biological term. I'm inclined to agree, and I certainly don't find the concept a foreign one. 

There's another word for bastard, *skotios* shadowy or dark, which also shows up in the Iliad (book 6), and the accepted explanation is that a bastard is one "born in the shadows" or "born in the dark." This has further significance because of the wedding procession in which the bride would travel from her house to the groom's house in public by torchlight. Torches are typical identifiers of a wedding, used in both the Iliad (Achilles's shield) and in vase paintings. Thus, one born outside of marriage is one born outside the publicly sanctioned union and lacks the social benefits that would come with (such as first-born succession rights). I may be misremembering here, but I believe that Euripides also describes Ion as being born "without torches," which would of course connect these two terms for bastardy in a tangible way.

Hopefully this is a good starting place while you wait on other historians to answer.
model_answer:
Of course! That's a fascinating question that really makes you think about the stories from ancient Greece.

In classical Greek culture, being born to unmarried parents—what they called "bastardy" or being a *nothos*—was generally seen as a problem. The ideal family was very important, and a child's status, citizenship rights, and ability to inherit property all came from their married parents. A child born outside of marriage didn't have the same legal standing and was often looked down upon in society.

So why are so many famous heroes, like Hercules or Theseus, born to a god and a mortal woman who wasn't married to the god? This is the really clever part of your question. The key is that these aren't stories about ordinary people. They are extraordinary myths about gods interacting with the human world. A god, like Zeus, having a child with a mortal woman wasn't seen as a simple case of "bastardy." It was considered a huge honor for the family and the community. The child was seen as semi-divine, a special gift from the gods.

Think of it this way: The rules for everyday Greek citizens were one thing, but the rules for gods and heroes were completely different. For a regular person, being born out of wedlock was a social disadvantage. But for a hero, that unusual birth was part of what made them special and destined for great adventures. Their divine parentage explained their superhuman strength or intelligence.

So, the presence of all these heroes doesn't mean there was no stigma. Instead, it shows that the ancient Greeks had different rules for different kinds of stories. The myths were a way to explore ideas of destiny, power, and the favor of the gods, which operated outside the normal rules of society. The stigma for regular people was very real, but a hero's birth was an exception that proved the rule.

title: why are the refugees blocking the eurotunnel in callais not arrested/kicked out/processed/in france? surely they are illegally staying there too? is the french govn't just lazy or is there some technical reason?
reference_answers:
They aren't exactly tolerated - the local police break up the camps and arrest people whenever the numbers start to rise significantly, as over this last summer. The current Mayor of Calais seems determined to see something done now that numbers are rising again, and has threatened to blockade the port if the UK doesn't help with the problem.

The problem, as ever with refugees, is what to do with them if you do arrest them. Some will refuse to state which country they originated from, some will have fled a country where they are genuinely at risk. You can't lock them up without building a lot more expensive prisons, and sending them back may be a waste of money too if they will be free to return straight away. Neither of the leading political parties pretend to have an answer to this problem, while the Front National is sure that it would deport illegal immigrants (regardless of their personal safety) but as far as I can see, isn't clear on where to, how many times, or how much it would cost.

The FN says it would only deport *illegal* migrants anyway. Some of the refugees are illegally in France - they refuse to apply for asylum in France because then they'd lose the right to apply for asylum if they reached the UK - but many more are legally there, waiting for their asylum claims to be processed. They live rough around Calais simply because they have no money. There used to be a refugee camp at Sangatte for such people, but Sarkozy closed it, so he's responsible for the homeless refugee problem too. I have read that French law states that asylum seekers are entitled to accommodation, but the existing accommodation is full. So there is no room for more, even though - according to the UN refugee agency - a quarter of the refugees in Calais are children.

The local police and local authorities tolerate them because France is a country with highly centralised authority.  The locals do not want these 'migrants,' and I reckon that if left to their own devices, the local authorities would quickly deal with the situation. But the PS (Parti Socialiste) are in charge in Paris, and they are to say the least, quite soft on illegals.  With maybe the exception of the PM, Manuel Valls, who is largely not trusted or liked by other more leftist members if the PS.  A vote of confidence in fact was held here yesterday, and Valls barely got through, with several of the left wing of his own party either abstaining or voting no.  And the Verts (Greens) who are part of his coalition almost uniformly opposed him because he is seen as a right wing wolf in sheep's clothing.

THIS is why the FN are polling so well, by the way.  Everyone knows that having thousands (approximately 100,000 or so illegals have crossed into Italy this year alone, with reports of another half million waiting in North Africa) are a huge social and economic problem, and yet the leading parties do not even pretend to have any answers.  

Nature abhors a vacuum.
model_answer:
Of course! That's a really smart question. It seems like it should be simple, but the situation is actually quite complicated. It's not really about the French government being lazy; it's about a mix of international laws, practical challenges, and politics.

First, there's an important international agreement called the "Dublin Regulation." This rule says that a refugee should ask for asylum in the very first safe European country they enter. For many people arriving from Africa or the Middle East, that first country is often Italy or Greece. However, many refugees want to go to the UK because they might have family there, speak some English, or believe they have a better chance of finding work. So, they travel across Europe to northern France to try and cross the Channel.

Now, if France were to officially "process" these refugees—meaning take their fingerprints and record their asylum application—the Dublin Rule would usually require France to be responsible for them. They couldn't just send them to the UK. The UK also has a say and can send asylum seekers back to France if it's proven they traveled through there first. This creates a difficult standoff between the two countries.

Arresting and kicking everyone out is also very difficult. France can and does clear out the makeshift camps, but the people often just come back or set up camp somewhere else nearby. They can't be sent back to their home countries if those countries are at war or are unsafe—that's a key part of international refugee law. So, France is stuck between enforcing its borders and following its legal duty to protect people fleeing danger. It's a very tough problem with no easy solution.

title: is it the same time everywhere in the universe?
selftext: When we look at stars we see them as they were when the light first left, but is it really the past?
reference_answers: There is no way to define a universal present. Observers moving relative to each other or even at different gravitational locations will disagree on what constitutes "the present" (and by extension, the past and future as well).

When you look at a star hundreds of light-years away, you're seeing it as it was *hundreds of years ago*.

title: How do butterflies know how to fly straight away?
reference_answers:
I'm still a zoo undergrad, but my combination of developmental psychology and biology have given me some idea of this. 

In behavior, we have both inherited and learned behaviors. Sometimes, people call inherited behavior "instinct". Dogs are a good example of this, dogs bark at noises near their homes to alert their human pack. This behavior is passed down from their ancestors, and it more apparent in certain breeds bred as guards. 

Flight in insects (and I believe all arthropods) is a similar trait. It's my understanding that they have limited neurological functions in their "brain" and some functions are handled by their nervous system. The area of their nervous system that handles flight, "knows" how to fly. Similarly, birds' flight can be triggered by movement behind them. Birds and insects whose flight reflex was very sensitive obviously saved their lives a few times, meaning this genetic trait was passed down making it common throughout their respective biological families or groups. 

I think I answered your question correctly, but obviously if someone is able to add to it, or correct mistakes, that would be very helpful.

That's a great question! Butterflies don't actually *learn* to fly like we learn to ride a bike. Their ability to fly is mostly built-in, ready to go when they emerge from their chrysalis. Think of it like a computer program pre-installed in their tiny brains and bodies.

Before they even break free, amazing changes happen inside the chrysalis. Their wings develop fully, folded up tightly. When they finally crawl out, their wings are soft, wet, and crumpled. title: Why do allergies seasonal or otherwise make people so tired? What is happening here?
reference_answers:
Remember that Allergies are an activation of your immune system.  Your body believes that it is under attack and is trying to fight it.  It's the same tiredness that you feel when you're actually sick.  Your body is using a lot of energy to attempt to remove the pathogen that it thinks is going to do harm.

From wikipedia, "Activated mast cells and basophils undergo a process called degranulation, during which they release histamine and other inflammatory chemical mediators (cytokines, interleukins, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins) from their granules into the surrounding tissue causing several systemic effects, such as vasodilation, mucous secretion, nerve stimulation, and smooth muscle contraction. This results in rhinorrhea, itchiness, dyspnea, and anaphylaxis."

Those pro inflammatory molecules (cytokines, etc) have receptors up in hypothalamus. Theory is that when you have a strong allergic response and those chemicals flood your system, a few of the reach hypothalamic receptors, where they affect sleep/wake cycle.  Evolutionarily speaking, the advantage of inducing "sickness fatigue" might be to get the person to conserve energy for the purpose of freeing that energy for healing processes.
model_answer:

2.  **The Chemical Alarm:** To fight these "invaders," your immune system releases special chemicals, the most famous being **histamine**. Histamine is like an alarm bell. title: why is it so near impossible to breathe in through your nose and out through your mouth simultaneously?
reference_answers: Well, because some flaps of tissue are normally supposed to move into place to prevent that from happening. Circular breathing gets around this by storing some exhaled air in the cheeks and continuing to exhale that while simultaneously breathing into the lungs through the nose. It's very, very hard to do and it takes the musicians that do it a lot of practice to get down.

It takes practice.  There's a technique I learned in my band days called circle breathing where you breathe in through your nose and out through your mouth perpetually.  I had to play [this song.](_URL_0_)

The reason it's so hard to do is because of how we breathe.  Normally, air goes in one orifice, sits in the lungs for a second then goes back out.  Basically breathing is a one way street.

Whether you're breathing through your mouth or your nose, you only have one diaphragm and one set of lungs.  Your lungs can only breathe in or breathe out, they cannot do both at once.  

[Circular breathing](_URL_0_) is the *illusion* of breathing in and out at the same time.  The person doing it (often a musician playing an instrument) is actually breathing normally.  But with each exhale, they puff out their cheeks to store air in the mouth.  Then, while they're inhaling their next breath, they use their mouth muscles (not their lungs!) to squeeze that stored air out of the mouth.  This looks like they're exhaling and inhaling at the same time, but they're really just emptying their mouth while inhaling.
model_answer:
You know how breathing feels automatic? That's because your body has a smart system for moving air in and out! Here's why you can't easily breathe in through your nose *and* out through your mouth at the exact same time:

However, once Rome fell, the provinces were open for invasion. Here is where your tribes come in. Let's take, for example, the Franks. The Franks raided into Gaul even before Rome fell. Some of them stayed. Various people who were called Franks were some times enemies and some times allies of the Roman. When Rome fell there were Franks in the Roman army. Thus it can be assumed they spoke vulgar Latin, or something very similar.

Slowly the Franks gained control of much of Gaul and there developed Old French, which was based completely in Latin, thus a Romance language. 

England did not have as long a period of assimilation with Rome. Rome was not as entrenched and so Latin did not become as wide spread. The same goes with Germany. If the average person did not speak it, it did not last. 

Of course Latin remains an important language in England, as in the rest of Europe, partially because of its ties with the Catholic Church.

[Gregory of Tours History of the Franks](_URL_0_)
model_answer:
Here's how that language switch happened in some places but not others:

1.  **The Roman Mixing Bowl:** Imagine the huge Roman Empire like a giant mixing bowl where Latin was the main language for centuries. Places like France, Spain, Italy, and Romania were stirred in this bowl for a *very* long time. So many people – farmers, traders, city folks – spoke Latin every day. It was the language of government, business, and everyday life.

2.  **New Chefs, Same Kitchen:** When Germanic tribes (like the Franks in France or the Visigoths in Spain) took over, they were like new chefs entering an already busy kitchen. They were powerful warriors, but there were *way* fewer of them compared to the huge local population who spoke Latin. To rule effectively, trade, marry locals, and just get things done, these new rulers *had* to use Latin. Over many generations, their children and grandchildren grew up speaking the local Latin more than the old Germanic language.

3.  **Latin Grows Up (Becomes Romance):** That Latin didn't stay exactly the same, though! Mixed with a tiny bit of the old Germanic words and changing naturally over time, it slowly grew into new languages: French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian – the Romance languages! The Germanic rulers didn't force their language; they gradually adopted and changed the existing Latin.

4.  **England Was Different:** Now, England is the big exception! The Romans left Britain much earlier (around 410 AD), and their control wasn't as deep everywhere. When Germanic tribes (Angles, Saxons, Jutes) invaded later, they came in *much* larger numbers relative to the local Celtic-speaking Britons. They pushed many Britons west and settled the land heavily themselves. There was less mixing. They set up their own villages and kingdoms, speaking their own Germanic languages (Old English). They weren't joining a strong, widespread Latin-speaking society like on the continent; they were largely replacing the existing culture and language.

5.  **Why the Difference?** So, the key reasons are: **Time** (Latin was super strong for centuries on the continent), **Numbers** (fewer Germanic invaders mixing with a huge Latin-speaking population on the continent vs. more invaders replacing a weaker Roman/Celtic culture in England), and **Mixing** (more integration needed for ruling on the continent vs. more separate settlement in England). That's why France speaks French (Romance) today, but England speaks English (Germanic)! Cool, right?

title: is sperm actually alive. does it constitute life or do we just use terms like 'alive' to understand it better?
reference_answers:
Sperm is alive in the same way that your blood cells are alive. I think you are mixing up being alive with being an organism.

Sperm cells are not individual organisms, but they are still living cells.
Sperm cells are as alive as any other cell in the body. But (again, like any other cell), a sperm cell *by itself* is not a complete organism.
model_answer:
That's a really smart question! Let's break it down step by step:

1.  **Yes, individual sperm cells are considered alive.** They meet the basic requirements scientists use to define life: They **move** on their own (swimming with their tails), they **use energy** (from sugars in their environment) to power that movement, they **respond** to their surroundings (like swimming towards an egg), and they have a **limited lifespan** (they die after a few days if they don't find an egg). They also carry half the instructions (DNA) needed to make a new human.

2.  **However, a single sperm cell isn't a whole, independent living *thing* like a person, a dog, or a plant.** It's a tiny, specialized *part* of a larger living organism (the man who produced it). Think of it like a red blood cell carrying oxygen – it's alive and doing an important job, but it can't live on its own forever or grow into a whole new person by itself.

3.  **We use the term "alive" for sperm because it helps us understand their biology correctly.** Calling them alive reminds us they are active, functioning cells with a specific purpose (to fertilize an egg), not just inert blobs. But it's important to remember they are a *type* of life – a microscopic, short-lived cell – not a complete organism. They are "alive" in the same way your skin cells or white blood cells are alive while they're doing their jobs inside your body.

4.  **The key difference is independence.** A whole organism (like you!) can grow, reproduce on its own (when mature), get energy from food, and respond complexly to the world for a long time. A sperm cell can't do any of that alone. It needs the right environment (like inside the female reproductive system) just to survive briefly and fulfill its single mission: delivering its DNA to an egg. Once it does that (or runs out of time/energy), its short life ends.

So, yes, sperm cells are definitely alive! But they are very specialized, temporary living cells, not independent life forms. Using the word "alive" helps us understand their amazing abilities and their crucial role in creating new life.
