title: Why Was HMS Hood Considered "Invincible"?
selftext: To add to the question above, considering the fate of the British battlecruisers at Jutland, why did HMS Hood enjoy such a favourable reputation, particularly vis-a-vis the Queen Elizabeth-class battleships, and considering it was never tested in battle?
reference_answers:
From [an earlier answer of mine](_URL_0_)

Flagships can be peculiar things in the twentieth century. Admirals sometimes chose flagships based on habit, others because the ship in questions had better communication equipment. Raymond Spruance preferred heavy cruisers likely for both reasons. Kurita Takeo's flagship before Leyte was the heavy cruiser *Atago*. He had to transfer his flag to *Yamato* after the submarine *Darter* sank her as the IJN taskforce was on its way to Leyte. So flagships are not necessarily the biggest and the baddest ships available. Some though were quite formidable and HMS *Hood* was one of them.  There were two reasons why HMS *Hood* earned this particular moniker "pride of the RN." 

One, HMS *Hood* was one of the more prominent ships within the public face of the RN in the interwar period. When launched, she was the largest and fastest capital ship  in the world. She held this record well until 1940 with *Bismarck*'s launching. Although Japanese and American battleships too would outshine *Hood* after *Bismarck*, the British battlecruiser was still among the most well-known ships in the fleet. One of the major duties of  HMS *Hood* was to serve as the flagship for a number of prestigious assignments such as the head of the Home Fleet's battlecruiser squadron or as flagship of the Mediterranean Feet. This gave her a very high visibility both among the British public and the world. The height of this visibility was arguably the 1923-1924 world tour in which the *Hood* was the flagship of a RN fleet that visited numerous ports around the globe as a gesture of goodwill. She actually was at the time the largest ship to ever traverse the Panama Canal and a number of ports on the tour were not deep enough to accommodate her draft. 

The second reason for HMS *Hood*'s public visibility was that she had little other competition within the interwar RN for the spot. Although she was a battlecruiser, she was better armored in many respects than the *Queen Elizabeth*-class battleships and faster. The only other capital ships the UK constructed before the "battleship holiday" of the Washington Naval Treaty were the [*Nelson*-class](_URL_1_) battleships. Although they had 16-inch guns and a decent armor scheme, they did not *look* like a battleship. They were squat, very slow (top speed was 23 knts), handled poorly, had an asymetiric main armament, and they looked like oilers with their aft-located superstructure. The *KGV*'s were new ships, but were also going through teething troubles. The RN was never quite able to make its quad 14" turrets work as promised and the battleships' design was somewhat compromised by trying to hew towards displacement limits set by the now-abandoned London Treaty. In short, HMS *Hood* beat its main rivals for being the most modern British battleship partly on aesthetic reasons. *Hood*'s clean lines, rakish bow, and symmetrical superstructure all screamed "battleship" while the *Nelson*s appeared to be the compromised design they were. 

The collapse of the naval limitation treaties did end the battleship holiday, but far too late for the RN. The *King George V*-class battleships began construction only at the end of the 1930s, so they would only be launched during the war. This meant these new ships had very little time to fix themselves in the public's eye. The advent of airpower and the gradual eclipse of the big guns as the main deciding factor in naval combat meant there was also not much for the *King George V*s to do during the war. HMS *Prince of Wales* had a highly visible career, but as part of failed missions: *Hood*'s attempt to stop the *Bismarck* where *PoW* was damaged, and as part of Force Z at Singapore where she was sunk along with HMS *Repulse*.

It's important to remember that *Hood* was just as well armoured as the *Queen Elizabeth* class battleships. Her 12in armour belt was only an inch thinner than that of the *Queen Elizabeth* class, but the slope of the armour made it equally effective. *Hood* also had a thicker upper belt than the *Queen Elizabeth*s, and an equally thick deck. The upper belt was the main weakness for both classes. She was also not considered invincible, at least not by the Royal Navy. Most discussions of *Hood* by RN officers focused on her poor protection, and there were frequent calls for her to be upgraded. There were plans for her to be upgraded in the 1940s, but shipyard space for this was not available before the Battle of the Denmark Strait. The upgrade would have fully extended her 12in belt, added more deck armour, and a more modern AA armament. 

Even the public did not feel that *Hood* was invincible. The public generally considered her beautiful, graceful, imposing, and a powerful symbol of imperial might. Hood was awe-inspiring in her might, in her size, and in her design; Ted Briggs, one of the three survivors of her sinking, described his first encounter with her:

 >  I stood on the beach for some considerable time, drinking in the beauty, grace, and immaculate strength of her. 'Beauty' and 'grace' seem rather ludicrous words to describe a vessel of such size, particularly one whose primary function was for destruction. But I can honestly say I never could, nor indeed can even today, think of more suitable words to describe her.

The look of a ship went a long way with the sailors of the RN, and with the general public, much more than the capabilities of the ship. A simple way to show this is to look at the nicknames the ships received. Nelson and Rodney, both more heavily armed and armoured than Hood, received the disparaging nicknames 'Nelsol' and 'Rodnol', because they resembled tankers in design. Ramillies, equally well-armed and armoured as Hood, was the 'One-funnelled Baa-Ram'. Hood was only ever 'the mighty Hood'.

Hood also, thanks to her cruises with the Battlecruiser Squadron, became a symbol of the might and power of the British Empire. Her first cruise was to Scandinavia, in 1920, but her more famous cruise was the 1923-4 World Cruise. Accompanied by Repulse, she visited the Empire's most important outposts, as well as ports in North and South America. In all these ports, she was a major attraction - at Melbourne, she was visited by 486,000 people in a week. She would visit more countries during her service in later years, especially during her Mediterranean cruises. These cruises turned her from a ship into a symbol; as V. C. Scott O'Connor would describe in his contemporary account of the World Cruise:

 >  In her mass and speed and perfection of armament, the Hood symbolises the valorous determination of war-weary Britain to maintain intact for the good of mankind the far-flung Empire she has built up through the centuries. It is this symbolism that lifts Hood out of the machine and irradiates the great grey hulk with a halo of splendour.
model_answer:
# Why Was HMS Hood Considered "Invincible"?

HMS Hood was never actually called "invincible" in an official sense, but she was definitely the pride of the Royal Navy! When she was completed in 1920, Hood was the largest warship in the world—longer than three football fields and absolutely massive. She was also incredibly fast for her size, which made her seem like a super-weapon. People loved her because she looked powerful and elegant, and she became a symbol of British naval strength, sailing around the world showing the flag.

Here's the interesting part about her reputation: you're absolutely right that British battlecruisers had exploded catastrophically at the Battle of Jutland in 1916, killing thousands of sailors. The problem was their thin armor—they were built for speed and big guns, but couldn't take hits well. Hood was actually *redesigned* after Jutland with much thicker armor, especially on her decks. This made people think she'd fixed the battlecruiser problem, combining speed with battleship-level protection.

However, Hood's reputation was partly based on appearance and hope rather than proof. She looked formidable and *seemed* better protected than the older battlecruisers, but she was never truly tested in major combat until 1941. The Queen Elizabeth-class battleships were actually more heavily armored in some ways, but Hood was newer, faster, and more famous. Her tragic fate against the Bismarck—sinking in minutes—showed that despite the improvements, she still had vulnerabilities, possibly in her deck armor where plunging shells could penetrate.

So Hood's reputation came from being big, fast, beautiful, and *seemingly* well-protected, combined with clever publicity and national pride—not from actual battle performance.

judge_result.comment: The answer is mostly accurate but lacks depth on Hood's armor and public perception compared to reference answers.

title: gravitational pull in relation to the ocean's tide...
selftext: I get what it does, but I've never really understood *how...*
reference_answers: [I wrote this a few days back](_URL_0_), let me know if anything needs clarifying.
model_answer:
# How Gravity Actually Pulls the Ocean

Great question! The "how" is actually pretty cool. Gravity gets weaker the farther away you are from something. So the side of Earth facing the Moon feels a *slightly* stronger pull than Earth's center does, and Earth's center feels a stronger pull than the side facing away from the Moon.

Here's the key part: the Moon pulls on the water, the solid Earth, and everything—but it pulls on each part with slightly different strength. The ocean water on the side nearest the Moon gets pulled a bit harder than the solid Earth beneath it, so it bulges outward toward the Moon. That's one high tide!

But wait—why is there *also* a high tide on the opposite side of Earth? Think of it this way: the solid Earth gets pulled toward the Moon more strongly than the water on the far side. So the Earth kind of gets pulled *away* from that far-side water, leaving it behind in a bulge. It's like the planet is being pulled out from under that water!

As Earth spins, different parts rotate through these two bulges, which is why most places get two high tides each day. The Sun does the same thing but with about half the effect, since it's much farther away. When the Sun and Moon line up, their effects add together and you get extra-high "spring tides"!

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains tidal mechanics with clarity and thoroughness, directly addressing the question about gravitational pull.

title: why does your appetite decrease in extreme heat?
reference_answers:
Your metabolism's job is to regulate the temperature of your body. "Metabolizing" food is basically like setting it on fire in your body and using the heat for energy. 

In the extreme heat, your body temperature is already high. So your body doesn't burn the energy it has as aggressively (your metabolism slows down) so that you don't overheat. This decreases your appetite.

It's also why you have less energy and feel wiped out after a hot day. You still needed that energy, but your body converted less to avoid overheating. Basically put you in low power mode.
Your body is a heater. It stays at 98.6°F like *all the time*. To keep it hot, you put food in it. If it is cold outside, you need more food. If it is hot, you need less.
TIL that people in texas are fat, because of heat-induced-slowed-metabolism, rather than because heat makes things expand...
model_answer:
# Why Does Your Appetite Decrease in Extreme Heat?

Great question! Your body is actually being pretty smart when it doesn't want to eat much on a super hot day.

Here's what's happening: Your body always tries to maintain a steady internal temperature of about 98.6°F (37°C), kind of like a thermostat keeping your house comfortable. When it's really hot outside, your body is already working hard to cool itself down through sweating and sending more blood to your skin to release heat.

Now, here's the key part: digesting food actually produces heat inside your body! It's called "thermogenesis," which just means "heat creation." When you eat, especially heavy meals with lots of protein and fat, your body has to work to break down that food, and this process generates warmth—like a little furnace inside you.

So when it's already blazing hot outside, your brain basically says, "We're overheating as it is—let's not add more heat by digesting a big meal right now!" That's why you naturally feel less hungry. Your body is trying to avoid making itself even hotter when it's already struggling to cool down.

This is also why you might crave cold, light foods like fruit or salads on hot days instead of hot soup or a heavy steak dinner. Your body knows what it needs! And staying hydrated with water becomes even more important than eating when it's extremely hot.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains the physiological reasons for decreased appetite in heat, is directly relevant, and is well-structured and clear.

Great question! You've stumbled onto something that puzzles a lot of people, and it's a really clever observation.

You're absolutely right that the laser dot on the moon would move incredibly fast! If you quickly rotate your laser pointer just a tiny bit, the dot could sweep across the moon's surface faster than the speed of light. In fact, people have calculated that with a small enough wrist flick, you could make the dot "travel" at many times light speed. So what's going on here?

The key is understanding what's actually moving. When you rotate the laser, you're not sending a single thing from one spot on the moon to another. Instead, you're pointing the laser at different places, and different photons (light particles) are hitting those different spots. It's like when you wave a water hose back and forth—the water droplets aren't zooming sideways at super speed; you're just spraying new droplets in different directions.

The speed of light rule says that no *information* or *matter* can travel faster than light. The laser dot isn't carrying information from one point to another on the moon—it's just an illusion of movement, like the lights on a theater marquee that seem to chase each other even though each bulb is just turning on and off in place.

So while the dot appears to move super fast, nothing is actually breaking the cosmic speed limit. Each individual photon still travels from Earth to the moon at exactly light speed, and no signal or object is actually racing across the moon's surface. It's a neat trick of perspective!

The lyrics to Twinkle Twinkle were indeed, as far as we know, written by Jane Taylor. The Wikipedia article shows she was born in London, which is near Colchester. Old King Cole's origins are very obscure and nobody knows who he really was. However, Geoffrey of Monmouth does associate him with Colcester by writing that he may have been King of Britons after the reign of the Romans ~300A.D. -Wikipedia, again. model_answer:
Great question! Yes, we do know the history of many nursery rhymes, though the stories are often murky and sometimes disputed—just like Colchester's claims!

**About Colchester's rhymes:** You're right that the Taylor sisters who wrote "Twinkle Twinkle Little Star" lived in Colchester in the early 1800s—that one's definitely true! However, the Humpty Dumpty cannon story is probably a myth. Historians haven't found solid evidence for it, and the rhyme doesn't actually mention Humpty being an egg or a cannon. As for Old King Cole, while there may have been a ruler named Coel in Roman Britain, we can't be certain the rhyme is about him since it was first written down much, much later (around the 1700s).

**Other rhymes we know about:** "Ring Around the Rosie" is often said to be about the plague, but that's almost certainly false—it's probably just a fun game song. "London Bridge is Falling Down" likely refers to real damage to London Bridge over centuries, though we're not sure which specific event. "Mary, Mary, Quite Contrary" might be about Queen Mary I of England and her troubled reign, though again, this is debated.

**The tricky truth:** Most nursery rhymes were passed down by word of mouth for generations before anyone wrote them down, so their true origins got lost or mixed up. People later invented explanations that sounded good but weren't necessarily true. It's like a very long game of telephone! Historians have to be detectives, looking at when rhymes were first published and what was happening at that time.

model_answer:
# Pedaling for Power: How Much Electricity Can You Make?

When you pedal a bicycle, your leg muscles are doing work, and that energy could theoretically be captured to generate electricity. A typical person cycling at a moderate, steady pace can generate about 75-100 watts of power. To keep things simple, let's say an average bicyclist produces about 75 watts while pedaling comfortably for 2 hours.

So how much electricity is that total? Power (watts) multiplied by time (hours) gives us energy in watt-hours. If you pedal at 75 watts for 2 hours, you'd generate 150 watt-hours, or 0.15 kilowatt-hours (kWh). That's the same unit you see on your family's electricity bill!

What could you actually power with that? Well, 150 watt-hours could run a laptop computer for about 2-3 hours, or keep a bright LED light bulb (15 watts) glowing for 10 hours. You could charge a smartphone about 10-15 times, or run a small TV for a couple of hours. It's enough to be useful, but not a huge amount.

To put this in perspective, the average American home uses about 30 kWh per day. That means you'd need to pedal for 2 hours every day for 200 days straight to power your house for just one day! This shows why we use power plants instead of bicycles for electricity—but it also shows that even small amounts of human power can charge your devices in a pinch.

title: What is wrong with the "Black Legend"?
selftext: As I basically understand it, the Black Legend formed as the rest of Europe learned about how oppressive the Spanish were to indigenous peoples.  Why is it considered to be an unfair representation of Spanish colonialism when objectively speaking the Spanish were very oppressive to indigenous peoples?
reference_answers:
Here's three things:

1. Most of the perpetrators of the Black Legend weren't simply saying "the Spanish are very oppressive to indigenous peoples." The Pope called them "the scum of the Earth." Immanuel Kant, in *Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime*, calls the Spaniard cruel, centuries behind in science, lazy, ignorant of reform, and un-European (derogatively). These are not objective utterances. Pope Paul IV, for instance, had what you might call a personal vendetta against the Spanish, having hated growing up there and being a political opponent of its royalty. Black Legend wasn't always a criticism of deeds, but the defaming of a people.

2. In modern popular accounts, criticism of the Spanish is typically tied with a hidden "noble savage" motif. The narrative is as follows: the Inca are living their happy peaceful life in the Andes. They've got a lot of cool things: roads with regular storehouses/rest stops, a diverse religious culture, nifty stoneworking techniques, etc. Then the white man comes with his horses and guns and tramples over them, forcing them to near slavery in tin and silver mines. Poor Inca! That was rightfully their land, and they never did anything to deserve that!
What's wrong with this? Any time you see this story, the Inca are the good guys and the Spanish are bad. As targustargus tried to point out, this completely lacks nuance and knowledge of Andean prehistory. For instance, the Inca were only native to the Cuzco area. They had conquered the rest of the Andes within the past hundred years, and they were still conquering places in the far north when the Spanish first arrived. Like the Spanish, they were a small ethnic group with big ambitions for conquest who laid their own culture and infrastructures on top of subjugated groups and who appropriated resources, culture, and religion for their own goals.
Additionally, the mit'a system you bring up was in fact an effective method of creating an infrastructure. In the Inca empire's brief existence though, this was often an infrastructure for conquest, with roads to facilitate troop movement and storehouses to extend campaigns. If a people joined the empire through treaty, then such a taxation might be reasonable. But if you're a former citizen of the enormous city of Chan Chan, defeated by Topa Inca Yupanqui's army ~1470, being forced to help replicate your own destruction is unspeakably humiliating. As an archaeologist of pre-Inca cultures, I am regularly frustrated by how much cultural knowledge has been lost due to the Inca conquest.

3. In addition, popular accounts focus on the Spanish actions and downplay native agency. It's always "The Spanish conquered the Inca" and it's never "The Inca attempted political intrigue and military outmanuevering against the Spanish, but failed." The conquest changed the Spanish as it did the Andeans.

**TL;DR Popular narratives downplay any benefits of the Spanish conquest and romanticize the prior Inca conquerors.**

Some good sources for complex looks at the conquest period:

Gose, P. (2008). Invaders as ancestors: on the intercultural making and unmaking of Spanish colonialism in the Andes. Toronto; Buffalo: University of Toronto Press.

Mumford, J. R. (2012). Vertical empire [electronic resource]: the general resettlement of Indians in the colonial Andes. Durham [N.C.]: Duke University Press.

Ramos, G. (2010). Death and conversion in the Andes: Lima and Cuzco, 1532-1670. Notre Dame, Ind.: University of Notre Dame Press.

Wernke, S. A. (2013). Negotiated settlements : Andean communities and landscapes under Inka and Spanish colonialism. Gainesville: University Press of Florida.
CommodoreCoCo has brought up some good point, but one thing I'd add is that the Black Legend is not about the brutality of European conquerors in the New World in general, but claims the Spanish were uniquely bad.

The Spanish did some bad things, but were they so much worse than the Dutch? The English? The French? The Portuguese?

In some ways, I would say they took different approaches. For example, the English were more likely to regard American Indians as being foreign states, while the Spanish were more likely to regard them as being Spanish subjects. Although thanks to the power differences, bigotry, etc, the Spanish authorities treated their Indian subjects worse than they treated, say, the typical Castilian peasant, and the English treated the Indian foreigners with more cruelty in war and less respect in peace than they did with, say, the Dutch when fighting the Anglo-Dutch wars or the treaties ending them. (This isn't to say that, say, the English never engaged in outright conquest, or that the Spanish never recognized the sovereignty of American Indian powers or signed treaties with them; just that the general patterns varied to some degree.)

Can we say the Spanish were *worse* though? That's a tougher call. From a sort of "international law" perspective, the Spanish approach of outright, often unprovoked conquest seems worse, but bringing people under the authority of the crown did give them some rudimentary sense of responsibility, whereas, say, the English coercing an Indian tribe into signing a "cede your land to us, and move somewhere else and starve to death" treaty felt much less responsibility.
model_answer:
Great question! You're right that the Spanish did terrible things during colonization—there's no denying that. The problem with the "Black Legend" isn't that it's completely false, but that it's *selectively* true in a way that's unfair and misleading.

Here's the issue: The "Black Legend" makes it seem like Spain was uniquely cruel and evil compared to other European colonizers. But the truth is that the British, French, Dutch, and Portuguese were *also* incredibly brutal to indigenous peoples. They enslaved people, spread diseases, stole land, and destroyed cultures too. The difference is that Spain's enemies (especially Protestant England and the Netherlands) heavily promoted stories about Spanish cruelty as propaganda to make themselves look better and Spain look worse.

Ironically, one reason we know so much about Spanish abuses is that some Spanish priests and officials (like Bartolomé de las Casas) actually *documented and criticized* what was happening. They wrote detailed accounts condemning the mistreatment of indigenous people. Other colonial powers didn't do this as much—not because they were kinder, but because they didn't have the same internal debate about it. So Spain's own records were used against them!

Think of it this way: imagine if one kid in class got called "the bully" because a teacher wrote down every mean thing they did, while other kids who were equally mean didn't get reported. The first kid *is* a bully, but it's unfair to act like they're the *only* bully. That's what's wrong with the Black Legend—it's not that Spain was innocent, but that singling them out as uniquely evil ignores how terrible colonialism was *everywhere*.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately addresses the Black Legend and its context, but lacks some nuance regarding indigenous agency and the complexity of colonialism.

model_answer:
# Why Don't Americans Eat Very Much Sheep?

Great question! Americans actually eat very little lamb or mutton (meat from sheep) compared to people in many other countries. There are a few interesting reasons for this.

**History and cattle culture:** When European settlers came to America, they found huge open spaces perfect for raising cattle. Cattle became king because cows give you both beef and dairy products, making them more valuable. The American West developed a strong "cowboy culture" around cattle ranching, not sheep herding. This meant beef became the default meat that Americans grew up eating and cooking.

**Taste and familiarity:** Lamb has a stronger, more distinctive flavor than chicken, pork, or beef. Since most Americans didn't grow up eating it regularly, many people find it unfamiliar or "too gamey" when they first try it. We tend to like foods we grew up with, so if your parents didn't cook lamb, you probably won't either. It becomes a cycle that continues through generations.

**Economics and availability:** Because fewer Americans buy lamb, grocery stores don't stock much of it, and it's usually more expensive than other meats. Farmers raise fewer sheep for meat since the demand is low. This makes lamb even harder to find and pricier, which means even fewer people buy it. It's a chicken-and-egg problem (or maybe a sheep-and-lamb problem!).

In contrast, countries like Australia, New Zealand, and many Middle Eastern nations have strong traditions of eating lamb, so it remains popular there. Culture and history really do shape what ends up on our dinner plates!

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains historical, cultural, and economic reasons for low sheep consumption in America.

title: why do you have to turn off your circuit breakers when starting electrical services?
selftext:
"To ensure your meter is turned on the day you request service, please make sure to turn off all circuit breakers in your home."  
I thought that by turning off your circuit breakers causes electricity to not flow, so why would they want me to turn it off? Is that not the opposite of what I want?
reference_answers: You turn off the circuit breakers so that there is no current flowing when the meter is being installed. If the line is hot, the technician sent out will probably not do it.
model_answer:
Great question! I can see why this seems backwards at first. Let me explain what's really going on.

When the electric company turns on your service, they're connecting your entire house to the power grid for the first time (or after it's been off). Imagine suddenly filling an empty garden hose with water at full pressure—there's a big rush all at once. The same thing happens with electricity. If all your circuit breakers are ON when they flip the main switch, every light, outlet, and appliance in your house would try to draw power at the exact same moment.

This sudden rush of electricity can create a power surge that might damage sensitive electronics like computers, TVs, or phone chargers. It's like a wave of electrical energy crashing through your house all at once. By having all the breakers OFF, you're making sure nothing is connected yet, so there's no surge when the power first arrives.

Once the electric company has safely connected your service, you can turn your circuit breakers back on one at a time. This way, you're gradually and safely bringing power to different parts of your house in a controlled manner. It's much gentler on your electrical system and your devices.

Think of it like this: the circuit breakers being OFF doesn't stop the electricity from reaching your house—it just stops it from flowing to your appliances and outlets until you're ready. The power company can still do their job of connecting you to the grid, and then you can safely distribute that power throughout your home when everything is ready.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains the need to turn off circuit breakers and is clear and well-structured.

title: why does lemon juice "cook" fish when making ceviche?
reference_answers: It doesn't actually cook the fish. The acid just denatures the proteins in fish meat in a similar process to cooking. It won't, for instance, kill pathogens in the fish.

Proteins are very long chains of a type of molecule called amino acid, hundreds or thousands of them. These chains tangle in a more or less random way (called protein folding), however organisms guide the tangling process so they end up in a specific shape that makes them useful.

When you apply heat to a protein, these chains will move, and if they become hot enough, they might untangle a bit and then tangle again, which can cause them to change their shape. This process is called "denaturisation", and is what makes meat, fish and egg change their colour and texture if you heat it up.

Acids like lemon juice will lower the forces that hold the chains together, which makes it easier to untangle them. Therefore, the temperature at which a protein will denaturate is lowered.

But as StupidLemonEater pointed out, this will not affect bacteria and parasites that can survive the stomach acid, which are usually killed off by high temperature. In that regard, you need to be just as careful as when you're making sashimi or carpacio.
model_answer:
# Why Lemon Juice "Cooks" Fish in Ceviche

Great question! When we make ceviche, the lemon or lime juice doesn't actually *cook* the fish with heat, but it does change the fish in a very similar way. The key is that the juice is very acidic, and acids can transform proteins just like heat does.

Fish meat is made of long protein molecules that are normally twisted and folded up in specific ways. When you apply heat (regular cooking), these proteins unwind and reconnect differently, which makes the fish turn from translucent and soft to opaque and firm. The acid in citrus juice does almost the same thing! It causes those protein molecules to unravel and tangle up with each other, changing the texture and appearance of the fish.

You can actually see this happening if you watch fish sitting in lime juice. After about 15-30 minutes, the fish starts turning white and opaque, just like it would if you cooked it in a pan. The acid is breaking down the protein structure. This process is called "denaturing" proteins, and both heat and acid can do it.

However, there's one important difference: acid doesn't kill bacteria and parasites as effectively as real heat does. That's why ceviche is traditionally made with very fresh, high-quality fish, and why you should be careful about where you get your fish if you want to make it at home. The acid changes the texture and appearance, but heat is still the best way to make fish completely safe to eat.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains the denaturation process and addresses safety concerns, providing a clear and thorough response to the question.

title: In The Good, The Bad and The Ugly, a character mislabels a union army because of dust on their uniform making him believe they are confederates. Did this ever happen in real life?
reference_answers: Misidentification wasn't uncommon, especially during the early days of the war when many units had different-colored uniforms. Notably, during the First Battle of Bull Run (July 1861), one of the turning points came when the 33rd Virginia (Confederate) regiment was mistaken for a Union unit. They were able to get close enough to decimate an infantry regiment and capture several artillery pieces, which (along with a charge by Stonewall Jackson and the arrival of some Confederate reserves) started the general Union retreat.
model_answer:
# Mistaken Identity in the Civil War

Yes, this kind of mix-up actually did happen during the American Civil War! The movie scene you're describing isn't just Hollywood drama—it's based on a real problem soldiers faced.

During the Civil War, uniforms weren't as standardized as you might think. Early in the war especially, both sides wore a variety of colors. Some Union soldiers wore gray, and some Confederate soldiers wore blue! Add in the dust, mud, and smoke from gunpowder on a battlefield, and it became really hard to tell who was on which side. Imagine trying to figure out if someone is your enemy or your friend when everything is covered in dirt and there's chaos all around you.

This confusion led to some tragic accidents. Soldiers sometimes fired on their own troops by mistake, or they held their fire thinking enemies were actually friends. One famous example happened at the Battle of Shiloh, where the confusion of battle and similar-looking uniforms caused friendly fire incidents. At the Battle of First Bull Run, a regiment wearing blue was actually fighting for the Confederates, which caused serious confusion.

Over time, both armies tried to fix this problem by making uniforms more consistent—Union in blue, Confederate in gray. They also started using flags, passwords, and other signals to identify each other. But especially in the dusty, smoky conditions of battle, mistaken identity remained a dangerous reality throughout the war.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains the issue of mistaken identity in the Civil War, providing relevant examples and clear context.

title: If the brain can't feel pain, why are aneurysms (sometimes) so painful?
reference_answers: The brain may not feel pain, but the dura mater, a sac that surrounds the brain, does. Any pressure on the dura can affect the trigeminal nerves and upper cervical nerves, causing extreme pain. I have intracranial hypertension, where I produce too much cerebrospinal fluid, so I was given a shunt to drain it. The shunt worked too well and created over drainage, which caused my brain to sink into my brain stem (called Chiari Malformation ). I was in severe pain due to the brains connections to the dura being pulled on, triggering the nerves and basically dropping me to my knees in pain multiple times a day. While not an aneurysm, the symptoms can be similar. I've had pressure headaches from having too much fluid, and headaches from not having enough. Hope that helps.
model_answer:
Great question! You're absolutely right that the brain itself can't feel pain—it has no pain sensors. That's why surgeons can operate on someone's brain while they're awake! But here's the twist: even though your brain can't feel pain, the structures *around* it definitely can.

When an aneurysm (a bulging, weakened spot in a blood vessel) happens in your head, it's not the brain tissue that hurts. Instead, it's the blood vessels themselves and the surrounding membranes that have pain sensors. Think of it like this: your brain is wrapped in protective layers called meninges, kind of like how a present is wrapped in paper. These layers, along with the blood vessels, are packed with nerves that can feel pain.

When an aneurysm bulges or—worse—ruptures (breaks open), it can stretch or tear these pain-sensitive blood vessels and membranes. If it ruptures, blood spills into the space around the brain, irritating those protective layers. This causes the sudden, severe headache that people often describe as "the worst headache of my life."

The pain can also happen because the swelling aneurysm presses against nerves near the brain, like the ones around your eyes or face. So while your brain itself is just sitting there feeling nothing, everything around it is sending urgent pain signals to let you know something is seriously wrong—which is actually a helpful warning system, even though it's incredibly uncomfortable!

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains pain mechanisms related to aneurysms and is clear and well-structured.

title: Roman slaves buying their own freedom
selftext:
We often read of Roman slaves in historical contexts being able to "buy their own freedom".  How did this work?  I'd have imagined that under slavery laws any possessions of a slave - for example his/her clothing - would have presumably belonged to the master.   

By extension any money owned by a slave would have already belonged to the slave's owner.  How then could a slave possess money independently to enable a purchase without that money already belonging to their master?
reference_answers:
It is true that anything the slave owned would have belonged to the master. Technically, the head of the family, the *paterfamilias* had the power over all the possessions of the people in his househould, under his *potestas*, excluding the wives' dowry (that is in a traditional *manus*-marriage, there were other forms of marriage that kept the possessions of both partners separate). So he was the sole legal owner of any and everything his wive, sons, daughters and slaves possessed until the time they left his power, since only persons who were *sui iuris*, of their own law, were able to own property. This is obviously a very unpracticable state of affairs.

The solution was not particular to slaves, but to all members of the familia who were under the power of the *paterfamilias*, and this was the concept of a *peculium*. In its original sense it is a special asset separate from other assets, in the common sense it meant those special assets that a *paterfamilias* entrusted to one of his subjects for them to work and manage, for example a small herd of animals, a building or plot of land and its profits, or a loan to run their own shop. *De jure* these assets are neither in the possession nor under the ownership of the holder of the *peculium*, their parts are still part of the assets of the owner. He or she only has *detentio*, that is the de facto possession and the ability to do with it what he wants. This has several advantages, for example it allowed sons to keep what they earned in the military (*pecunium castrense*) or through other service (*quasi castrense*); another advantage was that the master would not be liable with all his assets for the dealings that one of his slaves (or one of his profligate sons) undertook with the *peculium* entrusted to him, while still retaining possession of it; so a kind of ancient limited liability company, if you will. It also allowed the master to skim off the profits or dissolve the *peculium* at will. Since slaves were indispensable in the running of day-to-day business, this was an easy method to give them a freer hand, so they would need less control and could act on their own.

The biggest advantage in regard to slavery seems to have been that it provided a motivation for slaves to work hard for their master and profit from their own work. Varro in his treatise on agriculture, where slaves are discussed as part of the articulate tools needed to run a profitable farm, advises the farmer to give his slaves the opportunity to own some things of their own which they could profit from and use for their own goals.

 > They are made to take more interest in their work by being treated more liberally in respect either of food, or of more clothing, or of exemption from work, **or of permission to graze some cattle of their own on the farm, or other things of this kind**; so that, if some unusually heavy task is imposed, or punishment inflicted on them in some way, their loyalty and kindly feeling to the master may be restored by the consolation derived from such measures. [Varro, *rust.* 1.17, 7].

Having some cattle of their own to look after and profit from would have been a form of *peculium* fitting for a farm, and the word itself comes from the word for a small farm animal, *pecus*. So a slave could *de facto* have possessions of his own, even if they *de jure* belonged to his master, but there was a strong moral and economic obligation to honour this peculiar state of affairs, so it became common practice. I don't want to overstress the analogy, but in a certain sense it allowed the slave to become a share-holder in the masters enterprises, tying his economic success to that of his master. It seems obvious that this was a big motivation for the slave that was so minded to do his work well and look after his masters profits that thus became his own, in this limited way. 

It also seems that the *peculium* normally stayed with the slave when he was transferred to a new master:

 > In the purchase of slaves, it is customary for the peculium to go with the slave [Varro, *rust.* 2.10, 5]

Again, the important word here is customary, it was all up to the disposition of the master. He retained full ownership and could withdraw the *peculium* for any reason and at any time should he be so inclined, only facing the obstacle of overcoming common practices and mores, damaging his public image (which should not be underestimated in a society where people were so preoccupied with precisely that). What I want to say by this is that your mileage may vary, and if you are a slave on some far away plantation or any other remote place, who are you going to look for to complain? 

But, should the slave be freed at some point, he would also have retained possession and gained ownership of his allowance. In short, while a slave could not legally own anything, same as any other member of a household under the *pater*, there was *de facto* a possibillity to own and spend (and profit from) anything ranging from some pocket money or a small flock of sheep to a whole business operation. When Musicus Surranus, a slave of Tiberius, died some time in the 1st century, he was in possession of no less than sixteen under-slaves, or *vicarii* [see inscr. CIL VI 5197]. Slaves owning other slaves was another instrument to encourage loyalty and productiveness, and also competition among the slaves, something that might seem strange at first but makes perfect sense considering the things said above.

Now, as regarding buying their freedom, the evidence seems a bit mixed. It is certainly true that slaves *could* buy their freedom, like Publius Decimius Eros Mentula, who bought his for 50,000 sesterces [CIL XI 5400] and became a great and wealthy benefactor of his home town after this. But Mouritsen has recently argued [H. Mouritsen, The Freedman in the Roman World (Cambridge 2011), see here esp. p. 177ff.] that this was less often the case than is commonly assumed. One of his arguments is that there is less literary evidence for it than we like. The other, to me more convincing one is that it made less economic sense in the special context of Roman slavery.

It is true, buying your own freedom is a common staple of slaveholder societies ancient and modern, and a common trope, the deserving slave buying his own life back after hard work. However, the Roman freedman after his manumission still was in a very deep relationship with his former master, who now became his patron. Upon gaining his freedom, the slave took on the family name of his former master and thus became a full member of the masters family (and de facto this was one of the ways to perpetuate a family). One does only need to look at the way the Tulli Cicerones treated and cared for Ciceros slave and later freedman Tiro. He truly was family to them. Cicero and his brother Quintus in their letters show great concern both for Tiros health and well-being, but also for his professional success.

What this means is that, while the freedman still has obligations towards his patron, usually staying in his household and continuing to work for his former master in some capacity or another, the patron also has obligations to his client, to care for him and help him in times of need. Often freedmen would carry out their masters business interest, act as his authorized officers or trusted messengers and manage workshops or farms for him. Being the freedman of an important patron was an important position in and of itself, and the imperial freedmen running the emperors bureaucracy became a common trope in the 1st century. So, while it might not necessarily have served to buy his freedom directly, the *peculium* was the proof of a deserving slave, one who managed his own (and thus his master's) affairs well and worked hard, thus he was deserving of freedom. This might be where the connection between the *peculium* and manumission stems from. Simply taking back that *peculium* from the slave upon manumission would undermine that special 'social and moral bond' [Mouritsen 2011, 180] that would form the basis of their continued and important relationship, in which trust would play a very important part. 

One example of a type of slaves where the buying of ones own freedom was more common were actors and doctors (like Publius Decimius mentioned above), people who could make their own living with the specialist skills they had aquired without the support of their patron. Others might have been old or infirm slaves, who thus financed their replacement in a perverse twist of business acumen. But generally, other forms of manumission (by testament or for their hard service, or simply magnamity) seem to have been more common.

Edit: Added some stuff and fixed some typos/smoothed out the language a bit.
model_answer:
Great question! You've spotted something that seems like a logical puzzle, and you're absolutely right that it's a bit contradictory.

Legally, you're correct: slaves in ancient Rome couldn't truly own anything. Everything they had technically belonged to their master. However, Roman society developed a practical workaround called a "peculium" (peh-COOL-ee-um). This was like a personal allowance or fund that masters allowed their slaves to control and manage, even though it legally still belonged to the master. Think of it like when parents let kids manage their own piggy bank—the parents could technically take it back, but there's an understanding that they won't.

Slaves could add to their peculium in several ways. Some masters paid wages for extra work beyond regular duties. Skilled slaves (like teachers, doctors, or craftspeople) might earn tips or fees from other people. Some slaves ran small businesses on behalf of their masters and kept a portion of the profits. Over years or even decades, a hardworking slave might save up a substantial amount.

When a slave had saved enough, they could negotiate with their master to buy their freedom. The master would essentially be buying their own money back, which seems weird! But masters often agreed because: (1) they got a lump sum of cash immediately, (2) it encouraged their other slaves to work harder, and (3) freed slaves (called "freedmen") often continued working for their former masters anyway, now as paid clients. It was a system that, while still deeply unjust, gave some slaves a path to freedom—though it depended entirely on having a master willing to honor this informal arrangement.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains peculium and the process of buying freedom, but lacks some depth and nuance found in reference answers.

title: How was bastardy viewed in classical Greek culture? Does the presence of so many heroes born to unmarried parents suggest that there was no great stigma against it?
reference_answers:
As a linguist, I can tell you a little about one word in particular: *parthenios*.

*Parthenios* roughly translates as "bastard," but more accurately as "son of an unmarried woman." It is formed off *parthenos*, a term typically used of a virgin, but better translated as "young woman." Anyway, *parthenios* shows up in Iliad 16 when Achilles is choosing whom to send with Patroklus into battle. Of the men he chooses, two are described as children of immortal fathers (Menesthios and Eudoros) but only one is labeled a *parthenios* (Eudoros). Both women *are* married at the time in our story, so the difference seems to be whether the sons were conceived in or out of wedlock, regardless of the father. Menesthios was called a son of Boros (much like Jesus is the son of Joseph) while Eudoros is a *parthenios*. Homer tells us that Ekhekles pays many bride-gifts to marry Eudoros's mother (16.190), so it seems that there wasn't a penalty for her lack of virginity. It may be, though, that so long as the sexual activity and birthing is kept secret, then there is no penalty (Hermes lies with her in secret and Eudoros is left to his grandfather to raise).

This latter explanation holds some weight because in Euripides's *Ion*, we find Kreousa raped and then birthing in secret, and when she exposes Ion to the elements, she retains the adjective *parthenos*. (Maybe someone else can talk about this example though. I'm not well studied on Euripides.) Pindar in *Olympian* 6 calls Pitana a *parthenia* (daughter of unmarried woman) and mentions her hiding in her mother's robe.

Based on examples like these, the scholar Giulia Sissa is of the opinion that *parthenos* is a social status rather than a biological term. I'm inclined to agree, and I certainly don't find the concept a foreign one. 

There's another word for bastard, *skotios* shadowy or dark, which also shows up in the Iliad (book 6), and the accepted explanation is that a bastard is one "born in the shadows" or "born in the dark." This has further significance because of the wedding procession in which the bride would travel from her house to the groom's house in public by torchlight. Torches are typical identifiers of a wedding, used in both the Iliad (Achilles's shield) and in vase paintings. Thus, one born outside of marriage is one born outside the publicly sanctioned union and lacks the social benefits that would come with (such as first-born succession rights). I may be misremembering here, but I believe that Euripides also describes Ion as being born "without torches," which would of course connect these two terms for bastardy in a tangible way.

Hopefully this is a good starting place while you wait on other historians to answer.
model_answer:
# Illegitimacy in Ancient Greece

In ancient Greek culture, being born outside of marriage (what they called a "nothos") actually *was* a problem for regular people, even though many mythical heroes had unmarried parents. This might seem confusing at first, but there's a good explanation!

For ordinary Greek citizens, legitimate birth mattered a lot. In Athens, for example, only children born to two citizen parents who were properly married could inherit property or become full citizens themselves. If your parents weren't married, you might lose your inheritance, your right to own land, and your political rights. This was serious stuff that affected your whole life.

So why are so many heroes in Greek myths born to unmarried parents? Well, these stories usually involve a god (like Zeus) having a child with a mortal woman. The Greeks saw this differently than regular illegitimacy. When a god chose to have a child with someone, that was considered a special honor, not a scandal. The divine parent made the child extraordinary, not shameful.

Think of it this way: the myths were about explaining why certain heroes were so amazing and special—being half-god was the perfect explanation! But these stories didn't change the real-world rules for regular people. It's a bit like how superhero movies show people with powers doing things normal people can't do. The stories were inspiring and entertaining, but they didn't reflect everyday life or suggest that the usual rules didn't matter.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains the distinction between myth and reality regarding bastardy, but could include more specific examples from classical texts.

title: why are the refugees blocking the eurotunnel in callais not arrested/kicked out/processed/in france? surely they are illegally staying there too? is the french govn't just lazy or is there some technical reason?
reference_answers:
They aren't exactly tolerated - the local police break up the camps and arrest people whenever the numbers start to rise significantly, as over this last summer. The current Mayor of Calais seems determined to see something done now that numbers are rising again, and has threatened to blockade the port if the UK doesn't help with the problem.

The problem, as ever with refugees, is what to do with them if you do arrest them. Some will refuse to state which country they originated from, some will have fled a country where they are genuinely at risk. You can't lock them up without building a lot more expensive prisons, and sending them back may be a waste of money too if they will be free to return straight away. Neither of the leading political parties pretend to have an answer to this problem, while the Front National is sure that it would deport illegal immigrants (regardless of their personal safety) but as far as I can see, isn't clear on where to, how many times, or how much it would cost.

The FN says it would only deport *illegal* migrants anyway. Some of the refugees are illegally in France - they refuse to apply for asylum in France because then they'd lose the right to apply for asylum if they reached the UK - but many more are legally there, waiting for their asylum claims to be processed. They live rough around Calais simply because they have no money. There used to be a refugee camp at Sangatte for such people, but Sarkozy closed it, so he's responsible for the homeless refugee problem too. I have read that French law states that asylum seekers are entitled to accommodation, but the existing accommodation is full. So there is no room for more, even though - according to the UN refugee agency - a quarter of the refugees in Calais are children.

The local police and local authorities tolerate them because France is a country with highly centralised authority.  The locals do not want these 'migrants,' and I reckon that if left to their own devices, the local authorities would quickly deal with the situation. But the PS (Parti Socialiste) are in charge in Paris, and they are to say the least, quite soft on illegals.  With maybe the exception of the PM, Manuel Valls, who is largely not trusted or liked by other more leftist members if the PS.  A vote of confidence in fact was held here yesterday, and Valls barely got through, with several of the left wing of his own party either abstaining or voting no.  And the Verts (Greens) who are part of his coalition almost uniformly opposed him because he is seen as a right wing wolf in sheep's clothing.

THIS is why the FN are polling so well, by the way.  Everyone knows that having thousands (approximately 100,000 or so illegals have crossed into Italy this year alone, with reports of another half million waiting in North Africa) are a huge social and economic problem, and yet the leading parties do not even pretend to have any answers.  

Nature abhors a vacuum.
model_answer:
Great question! This situation is more complicated than it might seem at first.

First, you're right that many of these refugees don't have legal permission to stay in France. However, arresting and removing thousands of people isn't as simple as it sounds. Where would France send them? Many refugees have destroyed their identity documents, so it's hard to prove which country they're from. And even if France knows, those home countries often won't take people back without proper paperwork. It's like trying to return a package without an address.

Second, France *has* tried many times to clear these camps and move people along. Police have dismantled camps repeatedly over the years. But the refugees just set up again somewhere nearby because they're determined to reach the UK, where many have family or speak English. It's a bit like trying to sweep water uphill—it just flows back.

Third, there are legal and humanitarian issues. Under international law, refugees fleeing danger have certain rights. France can't just dump them at a border or put them on planes without following legal processes. These processes involve courts, paperwork, and appeals, which take time and money. Plus, many French organizations and citizens believe these people deserve compassion and help, which creates political pressure.

So it's not really about France being "lazy"—it's more that this is a really difficult problem with no easy solution. The French government is caught between wanting to enforce immigration laws, following international humanitarian rules, and dealing with the practical reality that these refugees are desperately trying to reach what they see as a better life in the UK.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately addresses the complexities of the refugee situation in Calais with clarity and thoroughness.

title: is it the same time everywhere in the universe?
selftext: When we look at stars we see them as they were when the light first left, but is it really the past?
reference_answers: There is no way to define a universal present. Observers moving relative to each other or even at different gravitational locations will disagree on what constitutes "the present" (and by extension, the past and future as well).
model_answer:
Let's talk about time and space. You know how we have clocks on Earth that show us what time it is, right? But, have you ever wondered if it's the same time everywhere in the universe? The answer is a bit tricky. You see, time is connected to how fast we're moving and where we are in the universe. It's not like there's a big clock in the sky that shows the same time everywhere.

When we look at stars, we see them as they were in the past. That's because light takes time to travel from the star to our eyes. For example, if a star is 10 light-years away, it means that the light we see from it today has been traveling through space for 10 years. So, what we're seeing is what the star looked like 10 years ago, not what it looks like right now. This is because light is like a messenger that carries information from the star to us, and it takes time for that message to arrive.

Now, you might be wondering, is it really the past that we're seeing? Well, kind of. From our perspective on Earth, yes, we're seeing the star as it was in the past. But, from the star's perspective, time is passing normally. It's not like time is standing still for the star just because we're seeing it in the past. It's more like we're getting a delayed message from the star, and that message is showing us what happened in the past.

This gets even more interesting when we think about how time works in different parts of the universe. According to a scientist named Albert Einstein, time can actually appear to pass differently depending on how fast you're moving and where you are in a gravitational field. For example, if you were to travel close to a black hole, time would appear to pass more slowly for you compared to someone who is far away from the black hole. It's a pretty mind-bending idea, but it's what our current understanding of the universe suggests.

So, to answer your question, it's not exactly the same time everywhere in the universe. Time is connected to our frame of reference, and it can appear to pass differently depending on our circumstances. But, that's what makes the universe so fascinating, right? There's still so much to learn and discover, and scientists are working hard to understand the mysteries of time and space.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains time's relativity and addresses the question clearly and thoroughly.

title: How do butterflies know how to fly straight away?
reference_answers:
I'm still a zoo undergrad, but my combination of developmental psychology and biology have given me some idea of this. 

In behavior, we have both inherited and learned behaviors. Sometimes, people call inherited behavior "instinct". Dogs are a good example of this, dogs bark at noises near their homes to alert their human pack. This behavior is passed down from their ancestors, and it more apparent in certain breeds bred as guards. 

Flight in insects (and I believe all arthropods) is a similar trait. It's my understanding that they have limited neurological functions in their "brain" and some functions are handled by their nervous system. This looks like they're exhaling and inhaling at the same time, but they're really just emptying their mouth while inhaling.

title: Why Was HMS Hood Considered "Invincible"?
selftext: To add to the question above, considering the fate of the British battlecruisers at Jutland, why did HMS Hood enjoy such a favourable reputation, particularly vis-a-vis the Queen Elizabeth-class battleships, and considering it was never tested in battle?
reference_answers:
From [an earlier answer of mine](_URL_0_)

Flagships can be peculiar things in the twentieth century. Admirals sometimes chose flagships based on habit, others because the ship in questions had better communication equipment. Raymond Spruance preferred heavy cruisers likely for both reasons. Kurita Takeo's flagship before Leyte was the heavy cruiser *Atago*. He had to transfer his flag to *Yamato* after the submarine *Darter* sank her as the IJN taskforce was on its way to Leyte. So flagships are not necessarily the biggest and the baddest ships available. Some though were quite formidable and HMS *Hood* was one of them.  There were two reasons why HMS *Hood* earned this particular moniker "pride of the RN." 

One, HMS *Hood* was one of the more prominent ships within the public face of the RN in the interwar period. When launched, she was the largest and fastest capital ship  in the world. She held this record well until 1940 with *Bismarck*'s launching. Although Japanese and American battleships too would outshine *Hood* after *Bismarck*, the British battlecruiser was still among the most well-known ships in the fleet. One of the major duties of  HMS *Hood* was to serve as the flagship for a number of prestigious assignments such as the head of the Home Fleet's battlecruiser squadron or as flagship of the Mediterranean Feet. This gave her a very high visibility both among the British public and the world. The height of this visibility was arguably the 1923-1924 world tour in which the *Hood* was the flagship of a RN fleet that visited numerous ports around the globe as a gesture of goodwill. She actually was at the time the largest ship to ever traverse the Panama Canal and a number of ports on the tour were not deep enough to accommodate her draft. 

The second reason for HMS *Hood*'s public visibility was that she had little other competition within the interwar RN for the spot. Although she was a battlecruiser, she was better armored in many respects than the *Queen Elizabeth*-class battleships and faster. The only other capital ships the UK constructed before the "battleship holiday" of the Washington Naval Treaty were the [*Nelson*-class](_URL_1_) battleships. Although they had 16-inch guns and a decent armor scheme, they did not *look* like a battleship. They were squat, very slow (top speed was 23 knts), handled poorly, had an asymetiric main armament, and they looked like oilers with their aft-located superstructure. The *KGV*'s were new ships, but were also going through teething troubles. The RN was never quite able to make its quad 14" turrets work as promised and the battleships' design was somewhat compromised by trying to hew towards displacement limits set by the now-abandoned London Treaty. In short, HMS *Hood* beat its main rivals for being the most modern British battleship partly on aesthetic reasons. *Hood*'s clean lines, rakish bow, and symmetrical superstructure all screamed "battleship" while the *Nelson*s appeared to be the compromised design they were. 

The collapse of the naval limitation treaties did end the battleship holiday, but far too late for the RN. The *King George V*-class battleships began construction only at the end of the 1930s, so they would only be launched during the war. This meant these new ships had very little time to fix themselves in the public's eye. The advent of airpower and the gradual eclipse of the big guns as the main deciding factor in naval combat meant there was also not much for the *King George V*s to do during the war. HMS *Prince of Wales* had a highly visible career, but as part of failed missions: *Hood*'s attempt to stop the *Bismarck* where *PoW* was damaged, and as part of Force Z at Singapore where she was sunk along with HMS *Repulse*.

It's important to remember that *Hood* was just as well armoured as the *Queen Elizabeth* class battleships. Her 12in armour belt was only an inch thinner than that of the *Queen Elizabeth* class, but the slope of the armour made it equally effective. *Hood* also had a thicker upper belt than the *Queen Elizabeth*s, and an equally thick deck. The upper belt was the main weakness for both classes. She was also not considered invincible, at least not by the Royal Navy. Most discussions of *Hood* by RN officers focused on her poor protection, and there were frequent calls for her to be upgraded. There were plans for her to be upgraded in the 1940s, but shipyard space for this was not available before the Battle of the Denmark Strait. The upgrade would have fully extended her 12in belt, added more deck armour, and a more modern AA armament. 

Even the public did not feel that *Hood* was invincible. The public generally considered her beautiful, graceful, imposing, and a powerful symbol of imperial might. Hood was awe-inspiring in her might, in her size, and in her design; Ted Briggs, one of the three survivors of her sinking, described his first encounter with her:

 >  I stood on the beach for some considerable time, drinking in the beauty, grace, and immaculate strength of her. 'Beauty' and 'grace' seem rather ludicrous words to describe a vessel of such size, particularly one whose primary function was for destruction. But I can honestly say I never could, nor indeed can even today, think of more suitable words to describe her.

The look of a ship went a long way with the sailors of the RN, and with the general public, much more than the capabilities of the ship. A simple way to show this is to look at the nicknames the ships received. Nelson and Rodney, both more heavily armed and armoured than Hood, received the disparaging nicknames 'Nelsol' and 'Rodnol', because they resembled tankers in design. Ramillies, equally well-armed and armoured as Hood, was the 'One-funnelled Baa-Ram'. Hood was only ever 'the mighty Hood'.

Hood also, thanks to her cruises with the Battlecruiser Squadron, became a symbol of the might and power of the British Empire. Her first cruise was to Scandinavia, in 1920, but her more famous cruise was the 1923-4 World Cruise. Accompanied by Repulse, she visited the Empire's most important outposts, as well as ports in North and South America. In all these ports, she was a major attraction - at Melbourne, she was visited by 486,000 people in a week. She would visit more countries during her service in later years, especially during her Mediterranean cruises. These cruises turned her from a ship into a symbol; as V. C. Scott O'Connor would describe in his contemporary account of the World Cruise:

 >  In her mass and speed and perfection of armament, the Hood symbolises the valorous determination of war-weary Britain to maintain intact for the good of mankind the far-flung Empire she has built up through the centuries. It is this symbolism that lifts Hood out of the machine and irradiates the great grey hulk with a halo of splendour.

title: What is wrong with the "Black Legend"?
selftext: As I basically understand it, the Black Legend formed as the rest of Europe learned about how oppressive the Spanish were to indigenous peoples.  Why is it considered to be an unfair representation of Spanish colonialism when objectively speaking the Spanish were very oppressive to indigenous peoples?
reference_answers:
Here's three things:

1. Most of the perpetrators of the Black Legend weren't simply saying "the Spanish are very oppressive to indigenous peoples." The Pope called them "the scum of the Earth." Immanuel Kant, in *Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime*, calls the Spaniard cruel, centuries behind in science, lazy, ignorant of reform, and un-European (derogatively). These are not objective utterances. Pope Paul IV, for instance, had what you might call a personal vendetta against the Spanish, having hated growing up there and being a political opponent of its royalty. Black Legend wasn't always a criticism of deeds, but the defaming of a people.

2. In modern popular accounts, criticism of the Spanish is typically tied with a hidden "noble savage" motif. The narrative is as follows: the Inca are living their happy peaceful life in the Andes. They've got a lot of cool things: roads with regular storehouses/rest stops, a diverse religious culture, nifty stoneworking techniques, etc. Then the white man comes with his horses and guns and tramples over them, forcing them to near slavery in tin and silver mines. Poor Inca! That was rightfully their land, and they never did anything to deserve that!
What's wrong with this? Any time you see this story, the Inca are the good guys and the Spanish are bad. As targustargus tried to point out, this completely lacks nuance and knowledge of Andean prehistory. For instance, the Inca were only native to the Cuzco area. They had conquered the rest of the Andes within the past hundred years, and they were still conquering places in the far north when the Spanish first arrived. Like the Spanish, they were a small ethnic group with big ambitions for conquest who laid their own culture and infrastructures on top of subjugated groups and who appropriated resources, culture, and religion for their own goals.
Additionally, the mit'a system you bring up was in fact an effective method of creating an infrastructure. In the Inca empire's brief existence though, this was often an infrastructure for conquest, with roads to facilitate troop movement and storehouses to extend campaigns. If a people joined the empire through treaty, then such a taxation might be reasonable. But if you're a former citizen of the enormous city of Chan Chan, defeated by Topa Inca Yupanqui's army ~1470, being forced to help replicate your own destruction is unspeakably humiliating. As an archaeologist of pre-Inca cultures, I am regularly frustrated by how much cultural knowledge has been lost due to the Inca conquest.

3. In addition, popular accounts focus on the Spanish actions and downplay native agency. It's always "The Spanish conquered the Inca" and it's never "The Inca attempted political intrigue and military outmanuevering against the Spanish, but failed." The conquest changed the Spanish as it did the Andeans.

**TL;DR Popular narratives downplay any benefits of the Spanish conquest and romanticize the prior Inca conquerors.**

Some good sources for complex looks at the conquest period:

Gose, P. (2008). Invaders as ancestors: on the intercultural making and unmaking of Spanish colonialism in the Andes. Toronto; Buffalo: University of Toronto Press.

Mumford, J. R. (2012). Vertical empire [electronic resource]: the general resettlement of Indians in the colonial Andes. Durham [N.C.]: Duke University Press.

Ramos, G. (2010). Death and conversion in the Andes: Lima and Cuzco, 1532-1670. Notre Dame, Ind.: University of Notre Dame Press.

Wernke, S. A. (2013). Negotiated settlements : Andean communities and landscapes under Inka and Spanish colonialism. Gainesville: University Press of Florida.
CommodoreCoCo has brought up some good point, but one thing I'd add is that the Black Legend is not about the brutality of European conquerors in the New World in general, but claims the Spanish were uniquely bad.

The Spanish did some bad things, but were they so much worse than the Dutch? The English? The French? The Portuguese?

In some ways, I would say they took different approaches. For example, the English were more likely to regard American Indians as being foreign states, while the Spanish were more likely to regard them as being Spanish subjects. Although thanks to the power differences, bigotry, etc, the Spanish authorities treated their Indian subjects worse than they treated, say, the typical Castilian peasant, and the English treated the Indian foreigners with more cruelty in war and less respect in peace than they did with, say, the Dutch when fighting the Anglo-Dutch wars or the treaties ending them. (This isn't to say that, say, the English never engaged in outright conquest, or that the Spanish never recognized the sovereignty of American Indian powers or signed treaties with them; just that the general patterns varied to some degree.)

Can we say the Spanish were *worse* though? That's a tougher call. From a sort of "international law" perspective, the Spanish approach of outright, often unprovoked conquest seems worse, but bringing people under the authority of the crown did give them some rudimentary sense of responsibility, whereas, say, the English coercing an Indian tribe into signing a "cede your land to us, and move somewhere else and starve to death" treaty felt much less responsibility.

title: why does lemon juice "cook" fish when making ceviche?
reference_answers: It doesn't actually cook the fish. The acid just denatures the proteins in fish meat in a similar process to cooking. It won't, for instance, kill pathogens in the fish.

Proteins are very long chains of a type of molecule called amino acid, hundreds or thousands of them. These chains tangle in a more or less random way (called protein folding), however organisms guide the tangling process so they end up in a specific shape that makes them useful.

When you apply heat to a protein, these chains will move, and if they become hot enough, they might untangle a bit and then tangle again, which can cause them to change their shape. This process is called "denaturisation", and is what makes meat, fish and egg change their colour and texture if you heat it up.

Acids like lemon juice will lower the forces that hold the chains together, which makes it easier to untangle them. Therefore, the temperature at which a protein will denaturate is lowered.

But as StupidLemonEater pointed out, this will not affect bacteria and parasites that can survive the stomach acid, which are usually killed off by high temperature. In that regard, you need to be just as careful as when you're making sashimi or carpacio.
