title: If the brain can't feel pain, why are aneurysms (sometimes) so painful?
reference_answers: The brain may not feel pain, but the dura mater, a sac that surrounds the brain, does. Any pressure on the dura can affect the trigeminal nerves and upper cervical nerves, causing extreme pain. I have intracranial hypertension, where I produce too much cerebrospinal fluid, so I was given a shunt to drain it. The shunt worked too well and created over drainage, which caused my brain to sink into my brain stem (called Chiari Malformation ). I was in severe pain due to the brains connections to the dura being pulled on, triggering the nerves and basically dropping me to my knees in pain multiple times a day. While not an aneurysm, the symptoms can be similar. I've had pressure headaches from having too much fluid, and headaches from not having enough. Hope that helps.
model_answer:
Let's talk about the brain and pain. You're right that the brain itself can't feel pain. This might sound a bit strange, but it's because the brain doesn't have the special nerve endings that detect pain, called pain receptors. These receptors are found in many other parts of our body, like our skin, muscles, and joints, which is why we can feel pain when we hurt those areas.

But, even though the brain can't feel pain directly, it can still be affected by things that happen inside or around it. An aneurysm is one of those things. An aneurysm is like a balloon that forms in a blood vessel, usually in the brain. When this balloon gets bigger, it can press on nearby nerves or tissues that do have pain receptors. It's kind of like when you press on a bruise – it hurts because you're putting pressure on the nerves in the bruised area.

When an aneurysm presses on these nerves or tissues, it can send pain signals to the brain, which interprets these signals as pain. So, even though the brain itself isn't feeling the pain, it's receiving the pain messages from the affected areas. This is why some people with aneurysms might experience really bad headaches or other types of pain.

It's also possible for an aneurysm to cause pain if it starts to leak or rupture. This can lead to bleeding in the brain, which can irritate the tissues and nerves around the aneurysm, causing even more pain. In severe cases, this can be a medical emergency that needs to be treated right away.

It's worth noting that not all aneurysms are painful. Some people might not feel any symptoms at all until the aneurysm gets bigger or starts to leak. But for those who do experience pain, it's usually a sign that something is wrong and they should see a doctor as soon as possible.

So, to sum it up, even though the brain can't feel pain directly, aneurysms can still cause pain by pressing on or irritating nearby nerves and tissues that do have pain receptors. This is why it's so important to listen to our bodies and seek medical help if we're experiencing severe or unusual pain.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains pain related to aneurysms, addressing the question clearly and thoroughly.

title: Roman slaves buying their own freedom
selftext:
We often read of Roman slaves in historical contexts being able to "buy their own freedom".  How did this work?  I'd have imagined that under slavery laws any possessions of a slave - for example his/her clothing - would have presumably belonged to the master.   

By extension any money owned by a slave would have already belonged to the slave's owner.  How then could a slave possess money independently to enable a purchase without that money already belonging to their master?
reference_answers:
It is true that anything the slave owned would have belonged to the master. Technically, the head of the family, the *paterfamilias* had the power over all the possessions of the people in his househould, under his *potestas*, excluding the wives' dowry (that is in a traditional *manus*-marriage, there were other forms of marriage that kept the possessions of both partners separate). So he was the sole legal owner of any and everything his wive, sons, daughters and slaves possessed until the time they left his power, since only persons who were *sui iuris*, of their own law, were able to own property. This is obviously a very unpracticable state of affairs.

The solution was not particular to slaves, but to all members of the familia who were under the power of the *paterfamilias*, and this was the concept of a *peculium*. In its original sense it is a special asset separate from other assets, in the common sense it meant those special assets that a *paterfamilias* entrusted to one of his subjects for them to work and manage, for example a small herd of animals, a building or plot of land and its profits, or a loan to run their own shop. *De jure* these assets are neither in the possession nor under the ownership of the holder of the *peculium*, their parts are still part of the assets of the owner. He or she only has *detentio*, that is the de facto possession and the ability to do with it what he wants. This has several advantages, for example it allowed sons to keep what they earned in the military (*pecunium castrense*) or through other service (*quasi castrense*); another advantage was that the master would not be liable with all his assets for the dealings that one of his slaves (or one of his profligate sons) undertook with the *peculium* entrusted to him, while still retaining possession of it; so a kind of ancient limited liability company, if you will. It also allowed the master to skim off the profits or dissolve the *peculium* at will. Since slaves were indispensable in the running of day-to-day business, this was an easy method to give them a freer hand, so they would need less control and could act on their own.

The biggest advantage in regard to slavery seems to have been that it provided a motivation for slaves to work hard for their master and profit from their own work. Varro in his treatise on agriculture, where slaves are discussed as part of the articulate tools needed to run a profitable farm, advises the farmer to give his slaves the opportunity to own some things of their own which they could profit from and use for their own goals.

 > They are made to take more interest in their work by being treated more liberally in respect either of food, or of more clothing, or of exemption from work, **or of permission to graze some cattle of their own on the farm, or other things of this kind**; so that, if some unusually heavy task is imposed, or punishment inflicted on them in some way, their loyalty and kindly feeling to the master may be restored by the consolation derived from such measures. [Varro, *rust.* 1.17, 7].

Having some cattle of their own to look after and profit from would have been a form of *peculium* fitting for a farm, and the word itself comes from the word for a small farm animal, *pecus*. So a slave could *de facto* have possessions of his own, even if they *de jure* belonged to his master, but there was a strong moral and economic obligation to honour this peculiar state of affairs, so it became common practice. I don't want to overstress the analogy, but in a certain sense it allowed the slave to become a share-holder in the masters enterprises, tying his economic success to that of his master. It seems obvious that this was a big motivation for the slave that was so minded to do his work well and look after his masters profits that thus became his own, in this limited way. 

It also seems that the *peculium* normally stayed with the slave when he was transferred to a new master:

 > In the purchase of slaves, it is customary for the peculium to go with the slave [Varro, *rust.* 2.10, 5]

Again, the important word here is customary, it was all up to the disposition of the master. He retained full ownership and could withdraw the *peculium* for any reason and at any time should he be so inclined, only facing the obstacle of overcoming common practices and mores, damaging his public image (which should not be underestimated in a society where people were so preoccupied with precisely that). What I want to say by this is that your mileage may vary, and if you are a slave on some far away plantation or any other remote place, who are you going to look for to complain? 

But, should the slave be freed at some point, he would also have retained possession and gained ownership of his allowance. In short, while a slave could not legally own anything, same as any other member of a household under the *pater*, there was *de facto* a possibillity to own and spend (and profit from) anything ranging from some pocket money or a small flock of sheep to a whole business operation. When Musicus Surranus, a slave of Tiberius, died some time in the 1st century, he was in possession of no less than sixteen under-slaves, or *vicarii* [see inscr. CIL VI 5197]. Slaves owning other slaves was another instrument to encourage loyalty and productiveness, and also competition among the slaves, something that might seem strange at first but makes perfect sense considering the things said above.

Now, as regarding buying their freedom, the evidence seems a bit mixed. It is certainly true that slaves *could* buy their freedom, like Publius Decimius Eros Mentula, who bought his for 50,000 sesterces [CIL XI 5400] and became a great and wealthy benefactor of his home town after this. But Mouritsen has recently argued [H. Mouritsen, The Freedman in the Roman World (Cambridge 2011), see here esp. p. 177ff.] that this was less often the case than is commonly assumed. One of his arguments is that there is less literary evidence for it than we like. The other, to me more convincing one is that it made less economic sense in the special context of Roman slavery.

It is true, buying your own freedom is a common staple of slaveholder societies ancient and modern, and a common trope, the deserving slave buying his own life back after hard work. However, the Roman freedman after his manumission still was in a very deep relationship with his former master, who now became his patron. Upon gaining his freedom, the slave took on the family name of his former master and thus became a full member of the masters family (and de facto this was one of the ways to perpetuate a family). One does only need to look at the way the Tulli Cicerones treated and cared for Ciceros slave and later freedman Tiro. He truly was family to them. Cicero and his brother Quintus in their letters show great concern both for Tiros health and well-being, but also for his professional success.

What this means is that, while the freedman still has obligations towards his patron, usually staying in his household and continuing to work for his former master in some capacity or another, the patron also has obligations to his client, to care for him and help him in times of need. Often freedmen would carry out their masters business interest, act as his authorized officers or trusted messengers and manage workshops or farms for him. Being the freedman of an important patron was an important position in and of itself, and the imperial freedmen running the emperors bureaucracy became a common trope in the 1st century. So, while it might not necessarily have served to buy his freedom directly, the *peculium* was the proof of a deserving slave, one who managed his own (and thus his master's) affairs well and worked hard, thus he was deserving of freedom. This might be where the connection between the *peculium* and manumission stems from. Simply taking back that *peculium* from the slave upon manumission would undermine that special 'social and moral bond' [Mouritsen 2011, 180] that would form the basis of their continued and important relationship, in which trust would play a very important part. 

One example of a type of slaves where the buying of ones own freedom was more common were actors and doctors (like Publius Decimius mentioned above), people who could make their own living with the specialist skills they had aquired without the support of their patron. Others might have been old or infirm slaves, who thus financed their replacement in a perverse twist of business acumen. But generally, other forms of manumission (by testament or for their hard service, or simply magnamity) seem to have been more common.

Edit: Added some stuff and fixed some typos/smoothed out the language a bit.
model_answer:
Let's talk about ancient Rome and how slaves could buy their own freedom. You're right to wonder how this worked, because it might seem like a paradox. If a slave's master owned everything the slave had, including their clothes and any money they might have, how could a slave possibly save up to buy their freedom?

The key to understanding this is to know that Roman law did allow slaves to have some possessions of their own, which were called "peculium." Peculium was like a special kind of savings account that a slave could have, and it was recognized by Roman law. The peculium belonged to the slave, but it was still under the control of the master. This meant that the master had to agree to let the slave use their peculium to buy their freedom.

So, how did slaves get money to put into their peculium? Well, some slaves were allowed to work on the side and earn extra money, which they could then put into their peculium. For example, a slave who was a skilled craftsman might be allowed to take on extra work in their free time and keep some of the money they earned. Other slaves might be given a small allowance by their master, which they could also put into their peculium.

As a slave saved up money in their peculium, they could eventually use it to buy their freedom from their master. This was called "manumission." When a slave was manumitted, they became a free person, and they could live their life as they chose. The master would often agree to manumit a slave in exchange for a certain amount of money, which the slave would pay using their peculium.

It's worth noting that not all slaves were able to buy their freedom, and the process of manumission was not always easy or straightforward. But for some slaves, having a peculium and being able to work towards buying their freedom was a powerful motivator, and it gave them a sense of hope and control over their lives. And that's a really important part of understanding what life was like for slaves in ancient Rome.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains peculium and manumission, but lacks depth on the complexities of slave ownership and economic motivations.

title: How was bastardy viewed in classical Greek culture? Does the presence of so many heroes born to unmarried parents suggest that there was no great stigma against it?
reference_answers:
As a linguist, I can tell you a little about one word in particular: *parthenios*.

*Parthenios* roughly translates as "bastard," but more accurately as "son of an unmarried woman." It is formed off *parthenos*, a term typically used of a virgin, but better translated as "young woman." Anyway, *parthenios* shows up in Iliad 16 when Achilles is choosing whom to send with Patroklus into battle. Of the men he chooses, two are described as children of immortal fathers (Menesthios and Eudoros) but only one is labeled a *parthenios* (Eudoros). Both women *are* married at the time in our story, so the difference seems to be whether the sons were conceived in or out of wedlock, regardless of the father. Menesthios was called a son of Boros (much like Jesus is the son of Joseph) while Eudoros is a *parthenios*. Homer tells us that Ekhekles pays many bride-gifts to marry Eudoros's mother (16.190), so it seems that there wasn't a penalty for her lack of virginity. It may be, though, that so long as the sexual activity and birthing is kept secret, then there is no penalty (Hermes lies with her in secret and Eudoros is left to his grandfather to raise).

This latter explanation holds some weight because in Euripides's *Ion*, we find Kreousa raped and then birthing in secret, and when she exposes Ion to the elements, she retains the adjective *parthenos*. (Maybe someone else can talk about this example though. I'm not well studied on Euripides.) Pindar in *Olympian* 6 calls Pitana a *parthenia* (daughter of unmarried woman) and mentions her hiding in her mother's robe.

Based on examples like these, the scholar Giulia Sissa is of the opinion that *parthenos* is a social status rather than a biological term. I'm inclined to agree, and I certainly don't find the concept a foreign one. 

There's another word for bastard, *skotios* shadowy or dark, which also shows up in the Iliad (book 6), and the accepted explanation is that a bastard is one "born in the shadows" or "born in the dark." This has further significance because of the wedding procession in which the bride would travel from her house to the groom's house in public by torchlight. Torches are typical identifiers of a wedding, used in both the Iliad (Achilles's shield) and in vase paintings. Thus, one born outside of marriage is one born outside the publicly sanctioned union and lacks the social benefits that would come with (such as first-born succession rights). I may be misremembering here, but I believe that Euripides also describes Ion as being born "without torches," which would of course connect these two terms for bastardy in a tangible way.

Hopefully this is a good starting place while you wait on other historians to answer.
model_answer:
Let's talk about ancient Greece. In those times, family and social status were very important. When we look at the stories of heroes like Hercules (or Heracles in Greek), Perseus, and Theseus, we notice that many of them were born to unmarried parents. This might make us wonder how the ancient Greeks felt about children born outside of marriage, which is sometimes referred to as "bastardy."

In ancient Greece, the family was seen as a crucial part of society. Marriage was not just about love between two people, but also about creating a family that would carry on the family name, inherit property, and perform important social and religious duties. Children born within a marriage were considered legitimate heirs and were entitled to certain rights and privileges. However, children born outside of marriage, like those of the heroes we mentioned, didn't always have the same rights and social standing.

Despite this, the presence of many heroes born to unmarried parents in Greek mythology doesn't necessarily mean there was no stigma against being born outside of marriage. In fact, in everyday life, there was a significant social stigma attached to being a child born out of wedlock. Such children might face difficulties in inheriting property, marrying well, or holding public office. However, the stories of these heroes are special because they are myths, meant to teach moral lessons or explain natural phenomena, rather than reflections of everyday life.

The reason we see so many heroes with unmarried parents in mythology is often because their stories were meant to emphasize their extraordinary nature. For example, Hercules was the son of Zeus, the king of the gods, and a mortal woman. This made him half-divine, which explained his incredible strength and bravery. The unusual circumstances of their birth often highlighted the heroes' special destinies and abilities. So, while being born out of wedlock might have been looked down upon in real life, in mythology, it could be a way to show that someone was extraordinary or chosen for great things.

It's also worth noting that ancient Greek society was complex, and attitudes towards children born outside of marriage could vary depending on the city-state (like Athens or Sparta) and the social class of the parents. However, in general, there was a preference for children to be born within a recognized marriage to ensure social stability and continuity of family lines. The stories of heroes, though, remind us that even in a society with strict social rules, there was room for stories of exceptional individuals who didn't fit the usual mold.

title: why are the refugees blocking the eurotunnel in callais not arrested/kicked out/processed/in france? surely they are illegally staying there too? is the french govn't just lazy or is there some technical reason?
reference_answers:
They aren't exactly tolerated - the local police break up the camps and arrest people whenever the numbers start to rise significantly, as over this last summer. The current Mayor of Calais seems determined to see something done now that numbers are rising again, and has threatened to blockade the port if the UK doesn't help with the problem.

The problem, as ever with refugees, is what to do with them if you do arrest them. Some will refuse to state which country they originated from, some will have fled a country where they are genuinely at risk. You can't lock them up without building a lot more expensive prisons, and sending them back may be a waste of money too if they will be free to return straight away. Neither of the leading political parties pretend to have an answer to this problem, while the Front National is sure that it would deport illegal immigrants (regardless of their personal safety) but as far as I can see, isn't clear on where to, how many times, or how much it would cost.

The FN says it would only deport *illegal* migrants anyway. Some of the refugees are illegally in France - they refuse to apply for asylum in France because then they'd lose the right to apply for asylum if they reached the UK - but many more are legally there, waiting for their asylum claims to be processed. They live rough around Calais simply because they have no money. There used to be a refugee camp at Sangatte for such people, but Sarkozy closed it, so he's responsible for the homeless refugee problem too. I have read that French law states that asylum seekers are entitled to accommodation, but the existing accommodation is full. So there is no room for more, even though - according to the UN refugee agency - a quarter of the refugees in Calais are children.

The local police and local authorities tolerate them because France is a country with highly centralised authority.  The locals do not want these 'migrants,' and I reckon that if left to their own devices, the local authorities would quickly deal with the situation. But the PS (Parti Socialiste) are in charge in Paris, and they are to say the least, quite soft on illegals.  With maybe the exception of the PM, Manuel Valls, who is largely not trusted or liked by other more leftist members if the PS.  A vote of confidence in fact was held here yesterday, and Valls barely got through, with several of the left wing of his own party either abstaining or voting no.  And the Verts (Greens) who are part of his coalition almost uniformly opposed him because he is seen as a right wing wolf in sheep's clothing.

THIS is why the FN are polling so well, by the way.  Everyone knows that having thousands (approximately 100,000 or so illegals have crossed into Italy this year alone, with reports of another half million waiting in North Africa) are a huge social and economic problem, and yet the leading parties do not even pretend to have any answers.  

Nature abhors a vacuum.
model_answer:
Let's break this down step by step. The refugees you're talking about are mostly from countries like Syria, Afghanistan, and Eritrea, and they're trying to get to the UK. They're gathering in Calais, France, near the Eurotunnel, which is a big tunnel that connects France and the UK under the sea. These refugees are trying to find a way to cross the tunnel or get on trucks and trains that are heading to the UK.

Now, you might wonder why the French government doesn't just arrest them or kick them out. The thing is, these refugees are seeking asylum, which means they're asking for protection from the French government because they're fleeing war, violence, or persecution in their home countries. Under international law, countries like France have to consider these requests and provide a safe place for these people to stay while their cases are being processed.

The problem is that the asylum process can take a long time, and there aren't enough resources or space to accommodate all these people. Many refugees prefer to try to get to the UK because they have family or friends there, or because they speak English and think they'll have a better chance of finding work and building a new life.

It's not that the French government is being lazy, but rather that they're dealing with a very complex and difficult situation. They're trying to balance the need to provide safety and protection to these refugees with the need to maintain order and security in the area. The French police and authorities are working to manage the situation, but it's a big challenge. They're also working with the UK government to find solutions, such as increasing security at the tunnel and providing more support for refugees who want to stay in France.

One technical reason why the refugees can't be simply "kicked out" is that France, like other European countries, has signed international agreements that protect the rights of refugees and asylum seekers. These agreements, such as the Geneva Convention, say that countries can't just send people back to places where they might face danger or persecution. So, the French government has to follow these rules and consider each person's case individually, which takes time and resources. It's a tough situation, but the goal is to find a fair and safe solution for everyone involved.

title: is it the same time everywhere in the universe?
selftext: When we look at stars we see them as they were when the light first left, but is it really the past?
reference_answers: There is no way to define a universal present. Observers moving relative to each other or even at different gravitational locations will disagree on what constitutes "the present" (and by extension, the past and future as well).
model_answer:
No, time isn't exactly the same everywhere in the universe. Clocks tick at different speeds depending on how fast something is moving or how strong gravity is pulling on it. This is from Einstein's ideas about relativity—if you're zooming near the speed of light or near a black hole, your clock runs slower compared to one on Earth.

When we look at stars or distant galaxies, we're seeing light that has traveled for years, thousands of years, or even billions of years to reach us. That light left the star long ago, carrying a picture of what the star looked like back then.

Yes, it really is the past! Those events—like a star exploding or twinkling—happened before the light started its trip. We're like detectives watching old home movies from across the cosmos; we can't see what's happening there right now, only what used to be.

Right now for us might not be right now for them, because "now" depends on where you are and how you're moving. But the starlight definitely shows history, not the present. Cool, right?

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains time differences and the nature of light from stars, addressing the question clearly and effectively.

title: How do butterflies know how to fly straight away?
reference_answers:
I'm still a zoo undergrad, but my combination of developmental psychology and biology have given me some idea of this. 

In behavior, we have both inherited and learned behaviors. Sometimes, people call inherited behavior "instinct". Dogs are a good example of this, dogs bark at noises near their homes to alert their human pack. This behavior is passed down from their ancestors, and it more apparent in certain breeds bred as guards. 

Flight in insects (and I believe all arthropods) is a similar trait. It's my understanding that they have limited neurological functions in their "brain" and some functions are handled by their nervous system. The area of their nervous system that handles flight, "knows" how to fly. Similarly, birds' flight can be triggered by movement behind them. Birds and insects whose flight reflex was very sensitive obviously saved their lives a few times, meaning this genetic trait was passed down making it common throughout their respective biological families or groups. 

I think I answered your question correctly, but obviously if someone is able to add to it, or correct mistakes, that would be very helpful.
model_answer:
Butterflies don't "learn" to fly like kids learn to ride a bike. Instead, flying is an instinct built right into their genes from millions of years of evolution. When a butterfly first comes out of its chrysalis, it's ready to fly almost right away—usually within a few hours—because its body is perfectly designed for it.

Right after emerging, the butterfly's wings are tiny and crumpled, like a wet paper fan. It pumps a special body fluid called hemolymph into the wings, which stretches them out to full size. Then, the wings dry and harden in the sun or air, kind of like how glue sets.

Once dry, the butterfly's brain and nerves take over. It has super-sensitive antennae to feel air currents and compound eyes that see movement all around. These senses, plus strong muscles in its chest, let it flap its wings up to 10 times a second. Instinct tells it exactly how to beat them to lift off and steer.

Its first flights might wobble a bit while it tests its wings, but soon it's zooming straight and steady. Nature wired butterflies this way so they can escape danger, find food, and even migrate right from the start!

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains butterfly flight instincts and processes clearly and directly, making it highly informative and relevant.

title: Why do allergies seasonal or otherwise make people so tired? What is happening here?
reference_answers:
Remember that Allergies are an activation of your immune system.  Your body believes that it is under attack and is trying to fight it.  It's the same tiredness that you feel when you're actually sick.  Your body is using a lot of energy to attempt to remove the pathogen that it thinks is going to do harm.

From wikipedia, "Activated mast cells and basophils undergo a process called degranulation, during which they release histamine and other inflammatory chemical mediators (cytokines, interleukins, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins) from their granules into the surrounding tissue causing several systemic effects, such as vasodilation, mucous secretion, nerve stimulation, and smooth muscle contraction. This results in rhinorrhea, itchiness, dyspnea, and anaphylaxis."

Those pro inflammatory molecules (cytokines, etc) have receptors up in hypothalamus. Theory is that when you have a strong allergic response and those chemicals flood your system, a few of the reach hypothalamic receptors, where they affect sleep/wake cycle.  Evolutionarily speaking, the advantage of inducing "sickness fatigue" might be to get the person to conserve energy for the purpose of freeing that energy for healing processes.
model_answer:
When you have allergies, like to pollen in spring or dust mites year-round, your body thinks the allergen is a dangerous invader, like a germ. It sends out special chemicals, mainly one called histamine, to fight it off. This causes sneezing, itchy eyes, and a runny nose to kick the "invader" out.

All this fighting tires your body out. The immune response—the team's big effort to protect you—uses up a lot of energy. Plus, the chemicals create swelling and inflammation, which makes everything feel heavy and drained, like after a long race.

You might not sleep well either. A stuffy nose means mouth breathing or waking up coughing, so you're extra tired the next day. Some allergy medicines block histamine but also make you sleepy on purpose.

Dehydration sneaks in too—from all the mucus or rubbing your eyes—which makes you feel sluggish. It's your body's way of saying, "Hey, take it easy while I handle this!"

judge_result.comment: The answer is mostly accurate and relevant, explaining fatigue from allergies well, but could include more detail on immune response mechanisms.

title: Is it true that Emperor Rameses 2nd had red hair? And if this is the case, where did he and the 19th Dynasty of Egypt come from?
selftext:
I was reading into a (psuedo)archaeological belief by [a collection of people who claim that New Zealand was previously populated by red-haired caucasians](_URL_1_), either Celts or an 
Indo-Aryan tribe from India, and that they are the reason why some (supposedly non-mixed) Maori [have striking red hair and green eyes](_URL_2_), as a documentary on the subject was just recently pulled from New Zealand television amidst a storm of criticism.

I was reading through this blog of people involved who made [claims that they found West Eurasian skeletons in some Northland caves that a university refused to have DNA tested](_URL_9_) (as usual psuedohistory tends to co-habitate with conspiracy theories about why it is not taken as standard history), but what caught my eye was the passing mention of a number of ancient historical figures in odd places who had red and blonde hair, and amongst them was the mention of [**Emperor Rameses II of Egypt, from 1300BC](_URL_7_). Thinking this a particularly conspiratorial idea, I googled Rameses II only to be shockingly surprised. Not only does his Wikipedia page give multiple sources confirming he had red hair, but numerous images also surfaced of the head of his mummy, which possesses a striking tuft of orange hair. The Wikipedia page also mentioned that he had an "aquiline nose" and likely came "from a family of redheads". In Ancient Egypt? 3300 years ago!?

[A picture of Rameses II's head with the hair in question. Redhead or Henna? Most sources I've come across state he was a natural redhead.](_URL_5_)

I had always assumed that red hair, alongside blonde hair and other fair hair-colours originated in Northern Eurasia, for both Neanderthals and Humans separately. Red hair is commonly associated with Celts, but moreso historical Indo-European speaking peoples such as [Ancient Slavs](_URL_0_), [Scythians](_URL_8_),  [Tocharians](_URL_6_) and the like, along with other groups like [Chechens](_URL_4_) and other peoples of the Caucasus, etc. are known for having a large number of red-haired people amongst their populations. Almost all of these people modern and historical are found in places nearby, or as a result of, [Indo-European migrations](_URL_3_) and also in Europe in g, though I think I read something recently calling this a dated assumption and that these hair colours originated in Central European farmers, I don't know. reference_answers: Not directly about Ramses, but /u/400-rabbits wrote [a post](_URL_0_) about other pseudohistorical claims about redheaded mummies in the Andes, where he(?) mentioned that reddening is a well known chemical process post mortem.

Many Mediterranean populations are believed to descend from the same proto-indo-european population that spawned the populations you speak of. Although rare, it is not unheard of for people in the Levantine region to sport red hair - the famous pirate and Ottoman admiral Oruç Reis, the original 'Barbossa' (italian for Red Beard - this name was carried to his brother after his death) reportedly sported a red beard, though other sources claim it was a mistranslation of his name. Regardless, Auburn hair is not considered odd in Turkish and middle eastern populations. On the other southern end of the Mediterranean, Berber populations of Morocco and Algeria frequently sport red hair even today. It should be noted that, as the gene responsible is recessive, naturally over time, it will become less common. As another user mentioned, the red coloring may be a side effect of mummification processes. 

I doubt very much these claims of a 'celtic' population reaching New Zealand in ancient times. An Indus river valley population migration is more plausible. I might propose European settlers of Australia being adopted to indigenous populations, or that it evolved independently, like [the naturally blond indigenous people of the Solomon Islands](_URL_0_). A genetic test would probably clear some questions. 

However, I'm not sure I understand the connection to Rameses; while Egypt is closer to NZ than, say Europe, it is still quite far away, with no indigenous populations of red heads appearing along any possible route taken

Ramses II, a famous pharaoh who ruled Egypt around 3,200 years ago, had a mummy with reddish-orange hair when it was discovered. But it's not true that he was a natural redhead like some people in Europe today. title: why is it so near impossible to breathe in through your nose and out through your mouth simultaneously?
reference_answers: Well, because some flaps of tissue are normally supposed to move into place to prevent that from happening. Circular breathing gets around this by storing some exhaled air in the cheeks and continuing to exhale that while simultaneously breathing into the lungs through the nose. It's very, very hard to do and it takes the musicians that do it a lot of practice to get down.

It takes practice.  There's a technique I learned in my band days called circle breathing where you breathe in through your nose and out through your mouth perpetually.  I had to play [this song.](_URL_0_)

The reason it's so hard to do is because of how we breathe.  Normally, air goes in one orifice, sits in the lungs for a second then goes back out.  Basically breathing is a one way street.

Whether you're breathing through your mouth or your nose, you only have one diaphragm and one set of lungs.  Your lungs can only breathe in or breathe out, they cannot do both at once.  

[Circular breathing](_URL_0_) is the *illusion* of breathing in and out at the same time.  The person doing it (often a musician playing an instrument) is actually breathing normally.  But with each exhale, they puff out their cheeks to store air in the mouth.  Then, while they're inhaling their next breath, they use their mouth muscles (not their lungs!) to squeeze that stored air out of the mouth.  This looks like they're exhaling and inhaling at the same time, but they're really just emptying their mouth while inhaling.
model_answer:
Imagine your lungs as a single balloon inside your chest. When you breathe in, your chest muscles expand to make the balloon bigger, creating low pressure inside. Air rushes in to fill it. When you breathe out, the muscles squeeze the balloon smaller, creating high pressure that pushes air out.

Your nose and mouth are like two different doors leading to the same hallway (your throat), which then goes straight to that balloon. Air from your nose flows through your nasal passages into the throat. Air from your mouth goes directly into the same throat spot.

To breathe in through your nose, you need low pressure in your lungs—air gets sucked in via the nose. But to breathe out through your mouth at the exact same time, you'd need high pressure to push air out the mouth. You can't have low and high pressure in the same balloon simultaneously—it's physically impossible!

Even if the pressures somehow matched, the air in your throat would just swirl around chaotically, with incoming and outgoing streams colliding. Your body isn't built with separate pipes for this; everything shares the same path.

That's why it feels impossible—your muscles and airways are designed for one-way flow at a time, keeping breathing simple and efficient. Cool, right?

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains the mechanics of breathing and directly addresses the question with clarity and detail.

title: Were free blacks during slavery better off than 'free' blacks during segregation?
selftext: I was recently watching 12 years a slave and during the opening scene it looked to me that the freed blacks seemed to enjoy almost perfectly equal status to the common white men - there were seemingly no separate facilities and they (seemed to be) treated as equals. Was this the case, or just how it's portrayed in movies?
reference_answers:
In a word, no.

First, remember that there was a great variation of standards of living depending on income, and location. Solomon Northrup's father was a property owner and he was relatively well educated. He likely was much better off than the average Negro at the time. The movie depicted an idyllic scene, but few, if any, whites in the 1830's would consider any black man an "equal", certainly there were friendships, but legally there was no comparison. 

Segregation was a step forward. Before "separate but equal" municipalities simply didn't offer those amenities for colored people. 

Southern freemen had it even worse. Some slave codes applied to free blacks as well, in some states it was illegal teach even free blacks to read. Freemen had to carry their papers at all times, and any white man could force any black man to show their papers. 

And, of course, there was always the specter of being kidnapped and sold into slavery just as Northrup was. 

"Free negroes belong to a degraded caste of society; they are in no respect on an equality with a white man. According to their condition they ought by law to be compelled to demean themselves as inferiors, from whom submission and respect to the whites, in all their intercourse in society, is demanded; I have always thought and while on the circuit ruled that words of impertinence and insolence addressed by a free negro to a white man, would justify an assault and battery" -Wilson, Black Codes (1965), p. 27. Quoting John B. O'Neall, Court of Appeals of South Carolina, in State vs. Harden (1832).

If you are really interested, I would suggest reading [The Black Codes of the South, by Theodore Wilson](_URL_0_).
model_answer:
No, free Black people during the time of slavery (before 1865) were not better off than Black people during the segregation era (roughly 1890s to 1960s). The movie *12 Years a Slave* shows a real but rare slice of life: it's set in New York, a Northern state where slavery was already illegal. There, free Black people like Solomon Northup could work, own property, and mix more freely with white neighbors—though they still faced prejudice and couldn't vote.

In the South during slavery, free Black people (about 250,000 by 1860) lived in constant danger. They had to carry special papers proving their freedom, follow strict curfews, and avoid being kidnapped and sold into slavery—like what happened to Northup. They couldn't testify in court against whites, own guns, or vote. Some ran businesses, but racism kept them unequal.

During segregation, called Jim Crow, things were legally worse in the South. Laws forced separate schools, buses, restaurants, and even water fountains for Black people—always inferior ones. Voting was blocked by tests and taxes, and lynchings (mob killings) terrorized communities. No slavery risk, but daily humiliation and violence were everywhere.

The movie's opening isn't how it was for most free Black people, especially in the South. Both eras were terrible, but segregation added harsh laws on top of the old racism. Freedom improved after the 1960s with civil rights laws.

judge_result.comment: The model's answer accurately compares the conditions of free Blacks during slavery and segregation, providing clear context and details relevant to the question.

title: Why does pain pulsate in intensity, and not remain consistent?
reference_answers:
Not all pain necessarily has the qualities of being pulsating/throbbing. 

Pulsating pain presents in a number of different pain conditions, but it has always been associated with some form of vascular involvement. The problem with this notion is that all that is 'obvious' is not always clear. 

In the case of headaches, while it has been shown that changes in intracranial pressure from coughing, bending/turning, etc. can affect pain intensity, recent research has been unable to establish direct evidence that the activation of mechanosensory afferents is in fact what produces the throbbing quality of pain.

*There is growing evidence the pulsating nature has much to do with how the pain is actually being processed (i.e. associations between alpha power fluctuations and the rhythm of throbbing events) instead of being a vascular phenomena.*

My knowledge of this area is mainly clinical so it would be great if we could get some others to weigh in on this subject from the research side.
model_answer:
Pain often throbs or pulses because it's tied to your heartbeat. Imagine banging your thumb—right away, it starts pounding in time with your pulse. This isn't random; it's your body's blood flow making it happen.

When you get hurt, the area swells up with extra fluid and blood to help heal it. Your heart pumps blood in strong bursts, so nearby blood vessels expand a little with each beat. That stretching presses on the sore tissues and nerves, ramping up the pain signal to your brain.

Between heartbeats, the pressure drops a bit, so the pain eases slightly. This on-off cycle matches your pulse—usually 60 to 100 times a minute—making it feel wavy instead of steady.

Not all pain pulses; a steady scrape might hurt evenly because there's less swelling or blood rush involved. Throbbing is your body's way of saying, "Hey, this spot needs attention!"

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains pulsating pain and its relation to blood flow, but lacks some depth on underlying mechanisms compared to reference answers.

title: How/why did the tribes who took over areas of the old Roman empire go from speaking Germanic languages to Romance ones? And why not in England?
reference_answers:
One must remember that when Rome fell, the people in the provinces did not simply disappear. They, for the most part, stayed right where they were. The people of Gaul spoke a vulgar form of Latin, but it had become region specific, displacing much of the Celtic languages that were there before. 

A linguist might be better suited to answer this question.

However, once Rome fell, the provinces were open for invasion. Here is where your tribes come in. Let's take, for example, the Franks. The Franks raided into Gaul even before Rome fell. Some of them stayed. Various people who were called Franks were some times enemies and some times allies of the Roman. When Rome fell there were Franks in the Roman army. Thus it can be assumed they spoke vulgar Latin, or something very similar.

Slowly the Franks gained control of much of Gaul and there developed Old French, which was based completely in Latin, thus a Romance language. 

England did not have as long a period of assimilation with Rome. Rome was not as entrenched and so Latin did not become as wide spread. The same goes with Germany. If the average person did not speak it, it did not last. 

Of course Latin remains an important language in England, as in the rest of Europe, partially because of its ties with the Catholic Church.


------------------------------------------
[_URL_1_](_URL_1_)

[Gregory of Tours History of the Franks](_URL_0_)
model_answer:
When the Western Roman Empire collapsed around 1,500 years ago, tribes from Germanic-speaking areas—like the Franks, Visigoths, and Ostrogoths—moved in and took control of places like France, Spain, and Italy. These invaders were warriors and leaders, but they were a small minority compared to the millions of local people who already lived there. Those locals spoke everyday Latin, the language of the Romans.

Over a few generations, the Germanic tribes switched to Latin because it was practical. They needed to talk with the locals for farming, trading, law, and church business. The tribes married locals, and their kids grew up speaking Latin at home and work. The old Germanic words faded away, and Latin slowly changed into new languages like French, Spanish, and Italian—we call these "Romance" languages because they come from Roman Latin.

England was different. When the Anglo-Saxons (another Germanic group) arrived around the same time, they came in bigger numbers relative to the locals, who were mostly Celtic speakers with some Latin. The Anglo-Saxons took over the countryside, pushed many locals aside or mixed less, and built their own farms and kingdoms. So, their Germanic language stuck and grew into Old English, which is why modern English feels more Germanic at its roots, even with later French influences.

judge_result.comment: The model's answer accurately explains language transition and differences in England, maintaining clarity and structure.

title: why are immigrants held at detention centers instead of being deported?
reference_answers: Laws state if they are not from Mexico, we cannot deport them to Mexico. Many of them only pass through Mexico.

The migrants being held at detention centers are seeking political asylum. They are being held until their claim to asylum is found valid or not. If it is found valid they are granted entry to the US if it is not found valid they are deported.
model_answer:
Immigration detention centers are like temporary holding places for people who enter a country without permission or break immigration rules. They're not prisons for criminals, but spots to keep people safe and organized while figuring out what to do next. Not everyone can be sent home right away.

Most countries, like the United States, have laws that give people a fair chance to explain why they should stay. This might include asking for asylum because they're scared of danger back home, or proving they have family or a job here. Judges review papers, hold hearings, and make decisions—it can take weeks, months, or even years.

Some people are held because they might run away before their case is done, or because they've done something dangerous. Detention helps make sure they show up for court. Others are released with rules, like checking in regularly, if they're not seen as a big risk.

Deporting someone immediately would skip these steps, which isn't allowed by law. It's like not letting someone tell their side of the story in a school fight. Once the process ends and they lose, they're sent back home. This keeps things fair and follows the rules.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains detention centers, legal processes, and the importance of fairness in immigration cases.

title: what are city states and how do they operate?
selftext:
I play a lot of Civ 5, a game where you play as a civilization and try to win by means of diplomacy, culture, science or military domination. They implemented city states into Civ 5, and I don't know what they are in reality and how they work. 

Are they just cities that grew so large that the government/country they would be part of decided not to govern them any more? Or did they get settled and decide not to be governed from the start?

Clarity edit: I want to know how they work in the real world, I understand how they function in Civ. I just can't wrap my head around how they function in reality.
reference_answers: Are you asking how the mechanics of city states works in the context of Civ 5?  Or are you asking what city states in real life are?  Two really different questions.
A City State is a city that has claimed it's own sovereignty - it's not part of any other country or empire.

In the world there are City-States, Nation-States, and Empires.

A real life city-state is an independent government, like a kingdom, able to feed, defend, and provide for its people. What makes it a city-state is that it is centered around only ONE city - along with the surrounding farmland and villages that sustain it. 

Many of the cities of Classical Greece were city-states, such as Thebes, Athens, Sparta, etc. Especially the island cities. In a city-state you might be friends with other cities, but you can act alone without a higher government than yours. 

You can also share a culture with other cities, and consider yourself part of a "nation" of people without being a part of a nation-state, like say France or like Greece is today.

In the case of America, the 50 States are actually operating as Nation-States which have agreed to answer to a higher government, based in Washington D.C.  Because of this, America (as "united states") is more of an Empire than a Nation-State.
A City State is much like any other country, just very small and with mostly only a city and maybe some suburb
model_answer:
City-states are like mini-countries that are just one big city and the land right around it. They run themselves completely independently, with their own leaders, laws, army, and money. Unlike in Civ 5 where they're smaller allies you can befriend, real city-states were powerful on their own and dealt with big empires as equals—or enemies.

They popped up in different times and places, like ancient Greece (Athens and Sparta), old Mesopotamia (cities like Babylon), or even Italy during the Renaissance (Venice and Genoa). Today, places like Singapore or Vatican City act a bit like modern city-states because they're tiny but super independent.

City-states worked by controlling trade, farming the nearby land, and building strong walls or navies for defense. Their leaders made all decisions locally—no far-off king bossing them around. They traded goods, formed alliances, or fought wars with neighbors to stay free and rich.

They didn't always form from cities growing "too big" for a country. Often, they started as busy ports or spots with great resources, like rivers or harbors, where people settled and built power from scratch. Sometimes they broke away from weak empires or stayed independent because they were too tough to conquer.

Most city-states didn't last forever—they got swallowed by bigger nations through war or teamwork. But they show how a smart, united city could thrive without being part of a huge country.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains city-states, their history, and operations, addressing the question clearly and thoroughly.

title: how do sodas travel the country all carbonated but as soon as you get one alone and it shakes up, its flat?!
selftext:
I’m confused and have been thinking of this for a while. They get shaken and dropped all across the country on their wooden pallets and in trucks and crates and are just fine. But as soon as you get one, of you shake it it gets flat! Is this like how when bicyclists ride bikes in close proximity, they use less energy or something? So maybe because all the sodas are all close together they absorb all the movement or something?! 

IDK! Lol just throwing it out there!
reference_answers:
When you shake a carbonated beverage, a bunch of the carbon dioxide which is the cause of the "fizz" goes out of the liquid and into the air.

If you then let it sit still for long enough, the carbon dioxide will dissolve back into the solution.

So if you shook a can of soda and let it be for a while (probably not even a day) the carbon dioxide will dissolve back into the soda and it'll be the same.

First off, you can't just drop a bottle of soda and have it be okay.  Try it out if you want, but I'm warning you, do it outside.  That being said, you can disturb them somewhat without losing it's fizzyness, as long as it remains sealed. 

Let's start with why soda is fizzy in the first place.  There is dissolved gas inside the liquid.  That gas doesn't like being there though.  It is constantly trying to escape out into the atmosphere.  In order for it to escape though, it needs two things: 

1) nucleation.  This just means it needs to be disturbed in some way.  Lot's of things can cause nucleation, such as microscopic scratches in the glass, but the most common, and the one we're concerned with is shaking and/or pouring.  When you move the drink, the gas gets disturbed, and can escape, as long as it has...

2) Space.  This is the key to why you can shake a closed bottle a bit, and it will still be fine. Even if you disturb the gas, if the gas has nowhere to go, it can't escape.  When a soda bottle is full, there is very little air in the bottle for the gas to escape to.  So when the bottle is filled, a little gas will escape the drink, but once that tiny space is full, that's it, no more gas can escape until the bottle is opened.

I would like to add that soda in its final form rarely if ever makes a cross-country trip. What happens with the big companies is they stir up the beverage base at their own place (this is JUST the flavorings and stuff), then ship *that* to the various regional bottling factories who then mix it with carbonated water, and then ship the final product out.

This is why when you see Coke and Pepsi delivery trucks, they're *always* driving a "day cab" semi, which doesn't have the sleeper area in the back. Don't need the sleeper area if you clock in make your rounds and clock out and go home each day.

Not sure if you've done high school chem covering equilibrium, but pretty much the carbon comes from a carbonic acid that can "transform" into carbon dioxide and water. This transformation is set to go towards an equilibrium state within a confined space and is influenced by factors such as temperature. For example all bodies of water are actually fighting to reach an equilibrium with vapor.

Water becomes vapor, and the higher the temperature, the more water will be vapor, the lower the temperature, the more vapor would be water. That's why clothes still dry when you hang them out despite it's no where near boiling temperature.

Inside a fixed volume such as that of the soda can, the acid won't have space to turn into carbon dioxide, therefore it won't "fizz". However if you get one alone and shake it up, you are stimulating the release of all of the carbon dioxide, and there will be no more acid in the soda. If the cap is on the bottle will bulge up and build up pressure, if the cap is off the gas will be released as quickly as possible.
model_answer:
Soda gets its fizz from a gas called carbon dioxide that's squeezed into the liquid under pressure inside the sealed can or bottle. That pressure keeps the gas dissolved, like how a sponge holds water until you squeeze it out. As long as the container stays sealed, the fizz stays locked in, no matter how much bumping around happens.

When sodas travel in trucks or on pallets, they're jostled a lot, but every single one is tightly sealed. Shaking mixes tiny bubbles into the liquid, but the pressure inside pushes them back into solution pretty quickly. They might slosh around during the trip, but the gas doesn't escape because there's no way out—until someone opens it later.

If you shake one soda can at home and then pop it open right away, those tiny bubbles expand super fast when the pressure suddenly drops. You get a big foamy spray, and some gas shoots out with it. That makes it seem "flat" because you've lost a bunch of fizz in the mess, but the rest of the soda is still carbonated—it just tastes less bubbly after that wild release.

The cans in shipping aren't opened during all that rough travel, so they arrive perfectly fizzy. Plus, stores usually let them sit still on shelves for a while before you buy one, giving any bubbles time to settle.

It's not like bicyclists drafting to save energy—sodas don't "help" each other stay fizzy when packed together. It's all about that strong seal keeping the pressure steady until you crack one open yourself!

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains carbonation, pressure, and the effects of shaking, addressing the question clearly and effectively.

title: is sperm actually alive. does it constitute life or do we just use terms like 'alive' to understand it better?
reference_answers:
Sperm is alive in the same way that your blood cells are alive. I think you are mixing up being alive with being an organism.

Sperm cells are not individual organisms, but they are still living cells.
Sperm cells are as alive as any other cell in the body. But (again, like any other cell), a sperm cell *by itself* is not a complete organism.
model_answer:
Sperm are tiny cells made in a man's body to help make a baby. Each one carries half of the instructions (like a blueprint) needed to create a new person. They have a head with DNA inside, a middle part for energy, and a whip-like tail to swim.

Yes, sperm are actually alive! Living things need a few key features: they use energy, they can move or react, they carry genetic information, and they come from other living things. Sperm do all that—they swim toward an egg using energy from sugars, respond to chemical signals, and have their own DNA.

We don't just call them "alive" as a shortcut; they really are living cells, like the cells in your skin or blood. But sperm are special—they can't grow, eat, or divide on their own. Their only job is to race to the egg and deliver DNA. Once they do that (and one fuses with the egg), they stop being sperm and help start a new life.

Outside the body, sperm die quickly without the right warmth and fluids, usually in hours or days. Inside, they live for a few days waiting for an egg. So, they're fully alive, but on a short mission!

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains sperm's characteristics and life status, directly addressing the question with clarity and detail.

title: why do we use wax instead of rubber to seal toilets to the floor drain?
selftext: The tank is attached with a rubber seal, why not the whole toilet?
reference_answers: I believe there are places that use rubber as well, but wax probably holds up over long periods of time.  Even high quality rubber tends to dry out over a long period of time, especially if it is constantly in an environment where it may go back and forth between wet and dry.

Toilet flanges are often really uneven, especially when on a concrete floor.  You need the wax to compress a LOT usually.  It will squish as much as a half inch, and it won't put any upward force on the toilet.  If you tried to compress rubber that much, you'd need to tighten the bolts on the toilet too much and it would crack the base.

Most forms of rubber will degrade over time from exposure to air, chemicals, and other "stuff" that goes down a toilet. Wax is incredibly stable stuff, and if you can avoid physically disturbing it (i.e. fasten the toilet correctly and firmly to the floor) it will hold up against extremely harsh cleaners, pressure from plungers, and even Taco Bell, often for decades.
They sell waxless seals at home improvement stores. I switched mine out when I upgraded the toilets. So far, so good.
model_answer:
Toilets connect to the floor drain with a soft wax ring, like a squishy donut made of beeswax mixed with other stuff. This ring sits between the toilet's bottom hole and a metal flange in the floor. When you bolt the heavy toilet down, the wax squishes flat and seals tight, blocking sewer gases and water leaks—even if the floor or toilet isn't perfectly smooth.

We use wax here instead of rubber because wax is super moldable under pressure. It smooshes into every tiny gap and stays put forever without rotting or shrinking. Rubber is bouncier and might slowly flatten out or get gooey from bathroom moisture and cleaners over years. Wax also doesn't let smells sneak up from the pipes.

The tank up top uses a rubber gasket (a bendy washer) because that's a different spot. The tank wobbles a bit when it fills with water and flushes, and rubber flexes without cracking. Bolts hold it snug, but not as crushingly tight as the base bolts. Rubber handles constant water contact better there too.

Some new toilets use rubber seals at the base now, but wax is still the go-to because it's cheap, easy to install by hand, and super reliable for most homes. It's like choosing peanut butter over jelly—both work, but wax sticks best where it counts!

judge_result.comment: The answer is accurate, directly addresses the question, and is clear and well-structured.

NPR stands for National Public Radio. It's a network of public radio stations across the U.S. that focuses on news, stories, and music without interrupting with ads trying to sell you stuff.

Unlike regular radio stations that make money by playing commercials, NPR is nonprofit. That means it doesn't chase profits for owners or shareholders. Instead, it gets most of its money from listeners like you and me who donate, plus grants from foundations and a little help from the government through the Corporation for Public Broadcasting.

NPR stations also get support from "underwriting" by companies. This is like a thank-you message at the end of a show, such as "Support for this program comes from [company name]." It's not an ad pushing a product—it's just info to keep things honest and independent.

title: Why Was HMS Hood Considered "Invincible"?
selftext: To add to the question above, considering the fate of the British battlecruisers at Jutland, why did HMS Hood enjoy such a favourable reputation, particularly vis-a-vis the Queen Elizabeth-class battleships, and considering it was never tested in battle?
reference_answers:
From [an earlier answer of mine](_URL_0_)

Flagships can be peculiar things in the twentieth century. Admirals sometimes chose flagships based on habit, others because the ship in questions had better communication equipment. Raymond Spruance preferred heavy cruisers likely for both reasons. Kurita Takeo's flagship before Leyte was the heavy cruiser *Atago*. He had to transfer his flag to *Yamato* after the submarine *Darter* sank her as the IJN taskforce was on its way to Leyte. So flagships are not necessarily the biggest and the baddest ships available. Some though were quite formidable and HMS *Hood* was one of them.  There were two reasons why HMS *Hood* earned this particular moniker "pride of the RN." 

One, HMS *Hood* was one of the more prominent ships within the public face of the RN in the interwar period. When launched, she was the largest and fastest capital ship  in the world. She held this record well until 1940 with *Bismarck*'s launching. Although Japanese and American battleships too would outshine *Hood* after *Bismarck*, the British battlecruiser was still among the most well-known ships in the fleet. One of the major duties of  HMS *Hood* was to serve as the flagship for a number of prestigious assignments such as the head of the Home Fleet's battlecruiser squadron or as flagship of the Mediterranean Feet. This gave her a very high visibility both among the British public and the world. The height of this visibility was arguably the 1923-1924 world tour in which the *Hood* was the flagship of a RN fleet that visited numerous ports around the globe as a gesture of goodwill. She actually was at the time the largest ship to ever traverse the Panama Canal and a number of ports on the tour were not deep enough to accommodate her draft. 

The second reason for HMS *Hood*'s public visibility was that she had little other competition within the interwar RN for the spot. Although she was a battlecruiser, she was better armored in many respects than the *Queen Elizabeth*-class battleships and faster. The only other capital ships the UK constructed before the "battleship holiday" of the Washington Naval Treaty were the [*Nelson*-class](_URL_1_) battleships. Although they had 16-inch guns and a decent armor scheme, they did not *look* like a battleship. They were squat, very slow (top speed was 23 knts), handled poorly, had an asymetiric main armament, and they looked like oilers with their aft-located superstructure. The *KGV*'s were new ships, but were also going through teething troubles. The RN was never quite able to make its quad 14" turrets work as promised and the battleships' design was somewhat compromised by trying to hew towards displacement limits set by the now-abandoned London Treaty. In short, HMS *Hood* beat its main rivals for being the most modern British battleship partly on aesthetic reasons. *Hood*'s clean lines, rakish bow, and symmetrical superstructure all screamed "battleship" while the *Nelson*s appeared to be the compromised design they were. 

The collapse of the naval limitation treaties did end the battleship holiday, but far too late for the RN. The *King George V*-class battleships began construction only at the end of the 1930s, so they would only be launched during the war. This meant these new ships had very little time to fix themselves in the public's eye. The advent of airpower and the gradual eclipse of the big guns as the main deciding factor in naval combat meant there was also not much for the *King George V*s to do during the war. HMS *Prince of Wales* had a highly visible career, but as part of failed missions: *Hood*'s attempt to stop the *Bismarck* where *PoW* was damaged, and as part of Force Z at Singapore where she was sunk along with HMS *Repulse*.

It's important to remember that *Hood* was just as well armoured as the *Queen Elizabeth* class battleships. Her 12in armour belt was only an inch thinner than that of the *Queen Elizabeth* class, but the slope of the armour made it equally effective. *Hood* also had a thicker upper belt than the *Queen Elizabeth*s, and an equally thick deck. The upper belt was the main weakness for both classes. She was also not considered invincible, at least not by the Royal Navy. Most discussions of *Hood* by RN officers focused on her poor protection, and there were frequent calls for her to be upgraded. There were plans for her to be upgraded in the 1940s, but shipyard space for this was not available before the Battle of the Denmark Strait. The upgrade would have fully extended her 12in belt, added more deck armour, and a more modern AA armament. 

Even the public did not feel that *Hood* was invincible. The public generally considered her beautiful, graceful, imposing, and a powerful symbol of imperial might. Hood was awe-inspiring in her might, in her size, and in her design; Ted Briggs, one of the three survivors of her sinking, described his first encounter with her:

 >  I stood on the beach for some considerable time, drinking in the beauty, grace, and immaculate strength of her. 'Beauty' and 'grace' seem rather ludicrous words to describe a vessel of such size, particularly one whose primary function was for destruction. But I can honestly say I never could, nor indeed can even today, think of more suitable words to describe her.

The look of a ship went a long way with the sailors of the RN, and with the general public, much more than the capabilities of the ship. A simple way to show this is to look at the nicknames the ships received. Nelson and Rodney, both more heavily armed and armoured than Hood, received the disparaging nicknames 'Nelsol' and 'Rodnol', because they resembled tankers in design. Ramillies, equally well-armed and armoured as Hood, was the 'One-funnelled Baa-Ram'. Hood was only ever 'the mighty Hood'.

Hood also, thanks to her cruises with the Battlecruiser Squadron, became a symbol of the might and power of the British Empire. Her first cruise was to Scandinavia, in 1920, but her more famous cruise was the 1923-4 World Cruise. Accompanied by Repulse, she visited the Empire's most important outposts, as well as ports in North and South America. In all these ports, she was a major attraction - at Melbourne, she was visited by 486,000 people in a week. She would visit more countries during her service in later years, especially during her Mediterranean cruises. These cruises turned her from a ship into a symbol; as V. C. Scott O'Connor would describe in his contemporary account of the World Cruise:

 >  In her mass and speed and perfection of armament, the Hood symbolises the valorous determination of war-weary Britain to maintain intact for the good of mankind the far-flung Empire she has built up through the centuries. It is this symbolism that lifts Hood out of the machine and irradiates the great grey hulk with a halo of splendour.
model_answer:
HMS Hood was a massive British warship built right after World War I, launched in 1918 and finished in 1920. At over 860 feet long and weighing more than 42,000 tons, it was the biggest battleship-like ship in the world back then. People called it "The Mighty Hood" or even "invincible" because of its huge size, blazing speed of 31 knots (about 36 miles per hour), and eight powerful 15-inch guns that could fire shells over 20 miles. It looked unbeatable, like a floating fortress.

But battlecruisers like Hood were tricky. Earlier ones, such as HMS Invincible, had exploded at the Battle of Jutland in 1916 because their armor was thin on top—like a strong helmet with a weak skull underneath. Enemy shells from far away plunged down and hit weak spots, causing huge blasts. Hood was designed smarter: it got thicker deck armor (up to 3 inches) and better protection overall, fixing those deadly flaws from Jutland. This made sailors and the public think it was now super-safe.

Compared to the Queen Elizabeth-class battleships, which had similar big guns but were slower (24 knots) and more heavily armored like true tanks, Hood shone in speed. It could chase down faster enemy cruisers or run from tougher battleships. The Queen Elizabeth ships were great for slugging it out, but Hood was the glamorous speed demon—the pride of Britain's navy during the peaceful years between wars.

Even without a real battle test until 1941, Hood's reputation soared. It cruised the world, showing off British power, and magazines called it invincible. No one had seen its weaknesses yet, so it stayed a symbol of might—until a lucky hit from the German ship Bismarck proved armor still had limits.

judge_result.comment: The answer is mostly accurate but oversimplifies armor details and lacks depth on public perception and historical context.

title: gravitational pull in relation to the ocean's tide...
selftext: I get what it does, but I've never really understood *how...*
reference_answers: [I wrote this a few days back](_URL_0_), let me know if anything needs clarifying.
model_answer:
The Moon's gravity pulls on everything on Earth, but it pulls a little harder on the ocean water that's closest to it. This makes the water bulge up into a high tide on the side of Earth facing the Moon.

On the opposite side of Earth, there's another bulge too. That's because the Moon pulls the whole planet slightly toward it, leaving the far-side ocean behind—like how you might swing a bucket of water and the water sloshes away from your hand.

Earth spins once a day, so most places get two high tides and two low tides every day as these bulges sweep past. The Sun adds its own pull, making super-high "spring tides" when it's lined up with the Moon.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains tidal mechanics clearly and concisely, addressing the question effectively.

title: why does your appetite decrease in extreme heat?
reference_answers:
Your metabolism's job is to regulate the temperature of your body. "Metabolizing" food is basically like setting it on fire in your body and using the heat for energy. 

In the extreme heat, your body temperature is already high. So your body doesn't burn the energy it has as aggressively (your metabolism slows down) so that you don't overheat. This decreases your appetite.

It's also why you have less energy and feel wiped out after a hot day. You still needed that energy, but your body converted less to avoid overheating. Basically put you in low power mode.
Your body is a heater. It stays at 98.6°F like *all the time*. To keep it hot, you put food in it. If it is cold outside, you need more food. If it is hot, you need less.
TIL that people in texas are fat, because of heat-induced-slowed-metabolism, rather than because heat makes things expand...
model_answer:
Your body is like a smart thermostat that works hard to stay at the perfect temperature—around 98.6°F (37°C). In extreme heat, it sweats a lot and sends extra blood to your skin to cool off. This uses up a ton of energy, so your body focuses on that instead of other jobs.

When you eat, your body has to digest food, which creates extra heat inside—like a tiny furnace. In scorching weather, your brain says, "No more heat, please!" It turns down your hunger signals to avoid getting even hotter.

Special brain chemicals help with this. One called leptin tells you you're full, and it ramps up in the heat. Another called ghrelin, which makes you hungry, drops. That's why you might skip meals without even thinking about it.

Sweating also makes you dehydrated, and when you're low on water, your appetite shrinks even more. Your body craves cool drinks over heavy food to stay safe and comfy.

judge_result.comment: The answer accurately explains appetite decrease in heat, covering metabolism, brain chemicals, and hydration clearly and effectively.

title: it is not possible to surpass the speed of light, but what happens if i point a laser from earth potent enough to reach the moon and just make a small shift from the source, the point in te moon would move much faster, right?
reference_answers: It wouldnt, photons are particles (sorta but its complicated). If the distance is far enough then think of it like water out of a hose. Even if you wave the hose around the water doesn't speed up, the particles just form an arc.

Aye, but the point on the moon does not actually exist -- it is not an object, only a series of different illuminations not connected to each other.

'Twas oft asked here. Ye may enjoy these:


1. [ELI5: Why A laser pointed at the moon doesn't move faster than light and break physics ](_URL_0_)
1. [ELI5: If I point a laser pointer at the moon and move my hand around very fast, what would happen to the speed of the dot on the moon's surface? ](_URL_3_)
1. [Please, ELI5, how can a shadow or spot move faster than the speed of light? ](_URL_2_)
1. [ELI5: If I point a laser to a wall far away enough and move that laser sideways so that the spot on the wall is moving fast enough, won't I be able to make the photons at the end of the laser go faster than light? ](_URL_1_)
model_answer:
That's a super clever question! It seems like if you wiggle a powerful laser pointer aimed at the Moon, the bright spot on the Moon's surface would zip across super fast—maybe even faster than light—because the Moon is about 240,000 miles away. A tiny shift at Earth would make the spot sweep a huge distance up there, right?

But here's the key: the spot isn't a real thing racing across the Moon. It's just where the laser light happens to hit at each moment. When you shift the laser, you're sending new beams of light in a slightly different direction. Each beam still travels from Earth to the Moon at the speed of light—nothing goes faster.

The spot looks like it's moving fast because the places where the light hits are changing quickly. It's like shining a flashlight on a far wall and swinging it: the shadow or spot slides across way faster than your hand moves. No actual stuff (like light particles or information) breaks the speed limit—it's all an illusion of the pattern shifting.

This doesn't break physics because nothing useful travels faster than light. You couldn't use it to send a message quicker than light speed. Cool experiment to think about, though—try it with a laser pointer and a wall!
